---
title: "Applied replication for data skills"
format: revealjs
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# All figures on these slides are generated here from the workshop data files
# (../data/*.csv) or from small inline tribbles of published summary values –
# no images of the Nature papers' figures are used (copyright + everything must
# stay editable). Palette mirrors style/cgm-slides.scss.
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(readr)
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
  library(purrr)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(dagitty)
  library(ggdag)
  library(patchwork)
})

ncl_blue <- "#0e3b6a"
orange   <- "#E69F00"
green    <- "#009E73"
d_red    <- "#a10000"
grey_mid <- "#848c94"

# A light slide-friendly ggplot theme: big type, no chart-junk.
theme_slide <- function(base_size = 17) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "grey90"),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ncl_blue),
      axis.title = element_text(colour = ncl_blue),
      legend.position = "none"
    )
}

# The four-cell repeatability matrix (Nosek et al. 2025). Defined once here so
# the full-colour slide and the 'robustness only' emphasis slide draw from a
# single source of truth – no copy-pasted plot code to drift apart. The data x
# analysis matrix is rendered as a tile grid (inline data, not a screenshot) so
# it stays fully editable; the term sits large in each cell with its one-line
# meaning beneath it.
repeatability_cells <- tibble::tribble(
  ~analysis,    ~data,       ~term,             ~def,                                  ~fill,
  "SAME METHODS",      "SAME DATA", "Reproducibility", "Testing the reliability of a prior finding\nwith the same data and same analysis\nstrategy by comparing the outcome of an\ninferential test as reported in a paper\nwith a re-calculation of that inferential\ntest from the original data.", "#0e3b6a",
  "DIFFERENT METHODS", "SAME DATA", "Robustness",  "Testing the reliability of a prior finding\nwith the same data and different analysis\nstrategy by conducting alternative\ntests on the original data.",  "#E69F00",
  "SAME METHODS",      "DIFFERENT DATA",  "Replicability",   "Testing the reliability of a prior finding\nwith new data expected to be theoretically\nequivalent by comparing the outcome of an\ninferential test as reported in a paper\nwith the equivalent inferential test as\ncalculated in the new dataset.",               "#009E73",
  "DIFFERENT METHODS", "DIFFERENT DATA", "Generalisability", "Testing the reliability of a prior finding\nin a new dataset in a way that differs\nfrom the original study but is expected\nto produce similar results.",                 "#834848"
)

# Draw the matrix. `highlight = NULL` keeps all four cells in full colour; pass
# a term (e.g. "Robustness") to dim every OTHER cell to a light-grey box. Text
# stays white throughout, so dimmed cells read as light-grey background + white
# text while the highlighted cell keeps its own colour.
repeatability_matrix <- function(highlight = NULL) {
  grey_box <- "#b6bcc3"   # light grey for de-emphasised cells
  cells <- repeatability_cells |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      data = factor(data, levels = c("SAME DATA", "DIFFERENT DATA")),
      analysis = factor(analysis,
        levels = c("DIFFERENT METHODS", "SAME METHODS")),
      fill = if (is.null(highlight)) fill
             else dplyr::if_else(term == highlight, fill, grey_box)
    )
  ggplot(cells, aes(data, analysis)) +
    geom_tile(aes(fill = fill), colour = "white", linewidth = 4,
              width = 1, height = 1) +
    geom_text(aes(label = term), colour = "white",
              fontface = "bold", size = 9, nudge_y = 0.25) +
    geom_text(aes(label = def), colour = "white",
              size = 5, nudge_y = -0.1, lineheight = 0.95) +
    scale_fill_identity() +
    scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_void(20) +
    # Row labels flipped to read vertically (bottom-to-top), matching the
    # rotated row-heads on the HTML image-grid version of this matrix.
    theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
          axis.text = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ncl_blue),
          axis.text.x.top = element_text(size = 17),
          axis.text.y = element_text(size = 15, angle = 90, hjust = 0.5),
          plot.margin = ggplot2::margin(2, 8, 2, 2))
}

# Read the two data files the multiverse slides depend on. Relative paths
# resolve from slides/ at render time (verified with quarto render).
# r_ca is the claim-aligned partial r – the day's convention: negative framings
# (mcomm, mlib, mneg) reverse-coded, so 'supports the claim' = negative sign
# for every outcome. All Part 4 curve/placement slides work on this scale;
# the class chart and the lab's percentile cell use the same one.
spec_grid <- readr::read_csv("../data/spec_grid.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::mutate(r_ca = ifelse(positive_outcome, r, -r))
analysts5 <- readr::read_csv("../data/analysts5.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# The 29 teams of Silberzahn et al. (2018), published values, read here because
# two slides in different parts draw them: the full forest in Part 1 and the
# one-row reminder strip in Part 2. Codebook: data/silberzahn29_codebook.md.
silberzahn29 <- readr::read_csv("../data/silberzahn29.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::mutate(distribution = factor(distribution,
                  levels = c("Linear", "Logistic", "Poisson", "Other")))

# Teams described their own methods and capitalised them 29 different ways;
# the published table title-cases them, and the forest slide follows suit.
tidy_approach <- function(x) {
  stringr::str_replace_all(stringr::str_to_title(x),
                           "\\b(And|A|For|With|Using|The|Of)\\b", tolower)
}

# Shared multiverse base layer. Built ONCE so the two consecutive multiverse
# slides ("The class multiverse" and "Where your result lands") are the
# SAME chart with an overlay, not two charts. The second slide calls spec_base()
# and adds the analyst lines on top: identical dims, axes, theme, zero line,
# baseline marker and legend slot, so the reveal animates lines appearing on one
# unchanging panel. coord_cartesian() pins the y-range so the overlay cannot
# rescale the axis between slides.
sc_ranked <- spec_grid |>
  dplyr::arrange(r_ca) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rank = dplyr::row_number())
sc_baseline <- dplyr::filter(sc_ranked, baseline)

spec_base <- function() {
  ggplot(sc_ranked, aes(rank, r_ca)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = grey_mid, linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = sig), size = 0.7, alpha = 0.55) +
    geom_point(data = sc_baseline, colour = d_red, size = 4) +
    annotate("text", x = sc_baseline$rank, y = sc_baseline$r_ca - 0.07,
             label = "constrained baseline\nt = −3.804",
             colour = d_red, fontface = "bold", size = 4, hjust = 0.15) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = ncl_blue, `FALSE` = "#c7ccd2"),
                        labels = c(`TRUE` = "p < .05", `FALSE` = "n.s."),
                        name = NULL) +
    labs(x = "specification (ranked by claim-aligned partial r)",
         y = "claim-aligned partial r") +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.75, 0.32)) +
    theme_slide(15) +
    theme(legend.position = "right", legend.title = element_blank())
}

# Fork-importance decomposition over the committed grid
# (data/fork_importance.csv: share of specification variance in partial r per
# menu axis, main-effects eta-squared). Read once; the Part 4 slide charts it.
fork_imp <- readr::read_csv("../data/fork_importance.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Analyst placement inside the 840-spec grid: the share of the grid more
# negative than each analyst's recorded partial r, on the claim-aligned scale
# (the analysts' own values are cosmopolitan-outcome results, so alignment
# leaves them untouched). The person/aggregate split is the published
# classification of the five Multi100 pipelines (KEVF1 and PRL47 fitted
# person-level models; the other three worked on aggregates).
an_level <- tibble::tribble(
  ~analyst_id, ~level,
  "KEVF1", "person-level",
  "PRL47", "person-level",
  "KQXUE", "aggregated",
  "018OL", "aggregated",
  "C6HJR", "aggregated"
)
an_placed <- analysts5 |>
  dplyr::left_join(an_level, by = "analyst_id") |>
  dplyr::mutate(pct_more_negative = purrr::map_dbl(r, \(x) mean(spec_grid$r_ca < x)) * 100) |>
  dplyr::arrange(pct_more_negative)

# Wrong-sign specifications in the cosmopolitan-only universe: the claim
# predicts a negative unemployment coefficient on mcosmo, so a positive
# estimate is a sign flip. Cross-tabbed by estimator and sample on the
# Part 4 patterned-flips slide.
flips_mcosmo <- spec_grid |>
  dplyr::filter(outcome == "mcosmo") |>
  dplyr::mutate(wrong_sign = estimate > 0)
```

2. The question underneath – one paper, five analysts, and what they were each asking
3. What you can actually do – reproduce a published result, then work the menu
4. Reading the multiverse – and choosing the one path you will defend
:::

:::

:::

::: notes
Welcome – good to have you here. A full day, in four parts of ninety minutes. The first part is the ground floor: what we are doing when we do social science, why people say it is in crisis, what open research proposes to do about that, and – because none of it happens without software – the tools. The second part goes inside one published paper that I re-analysed myself, and asks the harder question of why five analysts of the same claim came back with five different answers. The third part is the coding-heavy one: you reproduce my submitted result, then work through the menu of choices you could have made instead. And the fourth reads what the room built, and asks how you settle on the one analysis you would actually publish.
:::

## Two kinds of aim {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**What I want you to understand**

- What reproducibility, robustness and replicability each mean, and why they come apart
- Why analysts disagree – and how much of that is disagreement about the *question*
- What a causal graph buys you when you cannot make a causal claim
- What a multiverse shows, and what it cannot show
- What preregistration settles, and what it leaves open
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**What I want you to be able to do**

- Get an analysis running from someone else's materials
- Write an estimand in one sentence, and a DAG that matches it
- Reproduce a published result to the third decimal
- Vary a specification deliberately and read what changed
- Declare an analysis before you run it, and report where it sits among the alternatives
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
Two columns, because the day has two kinds of aim and they are not the same thing. On the left is what I want you to understand – conceptual work, and most of it is not about code at all. On the right is what I want you to be able to do by six o'clock, and every one of those is something you will have done at least once today with your own hands. If you only take the left-hand column home you will have had an interesting day and changed nothing about your practice. If you only take the right-hand column you will have learned some R. The point is the pairing: the concepts tell you which of the things you can now do is worth doing.
:::

# PART 1 – Why any of this, and with what tools {.darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 1 · 90 minutes
:::

::: notes
Part one, then. We start further back than you might expect, with what science is for and why anyone thinks it is in trouble. Then what open research proposes as the remedy, and how well that holds up. Then the evidence: three enormous studies published together this year that put numbers on how often social-science findings survive being repeated. Then a first look at the one of those studies I was inside. And we finish on the tools, because every part of this – the sharing, the checking, the repeating – is something software either makes easy or makes impossible.
:::

## What are we doing when we do social science?

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Making **claims about the world** that could turn out to be wrong – and saying how we would know.
:::

::: {.fragment}
A claim is not private. It is offered to others so they can **check it, use it, argue with it, build on it**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
That handover is the whole enterprise. Everything today is about whether it works.
:::
::::

::: notes
Start with the obvious question that nobody asks out loud. What are we actually doing? We are making claims about the world – claims that could turn out to be wrong, and that come with some statement of how we would find out. And crucially, a claim is not a private possession. You publish it so that other people can check it, use it, argue with it, and build on top of it. That handover is not an administrative afterthought; it is the entire enterprise. A finding nobody else can examine is not a contribution, it is an assertion. So when we ask today whether social science is in trouble, the question is really quite specific: does the handover work? Can someone else pick your finding up and do anything with it?
:::

## Three arguments that made people nervous {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- **The theory, 2005.** With small studies, small true effects, flexible designs and many teams chasing the same question, most published findings in a field can be false with nobody breaking any rules [@Ioannidis2005WhyMostPublished]
- **The demonstration, 2011.** Give researchers only the flexibility they legitimately have – which cases to drop, which covariates to keep, when to stop collecting – and a **false-positive rate of 5% becomes over 60%** [@SimmonsEtAl2011FalsePositivePsychology]
- **The subtlety, 2014.** You do not need many tests. In a **garden of forking paths**, a single test *chosen after looking at the data* already has the wrong p-value [@GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience]
:::

::: notes
Three arguments, in order of how uncomfortable they are. Ioannidis in 2005 made the theoretical case: put together small studies, small true effects, flexible designs and lots of teams chasing the same question, and you can show that most published findings in a field will be false without anybody breaking a single rule. Then Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn demonstrated it in practice – give researchers only the flexibility they legitimately have, and you can push a five per cent false-positive rate above sixty. They proved it by 'showing', with real participants and real statistics, that listening to a Beatles song makes you younger. And Gelman and Loken added the subtlety that I find hardest to shake: you do not have to run many tests for this to bite. If the one test you ran was chosen after you looked at the data, its p-value is already wrong.
:::

## And then people counted {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- **100 psychology experiments**, replicated with high power and the original materials: **97%** of the originals were significant, **36%** of the replications were, and effect sizes roughly **halved** [@OpenScienceCollaboration2015EstimatingReproducibilityPsychological]
- **161 researchers, 73 teams, one hypothesis** on immigration and support for social policy: **1,253** models, and no convergence on either sign or significance [@BreznauEtAl2022ObservingManyResearchers]
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Different fields, different designs, one uncomfortable conclusion: **the finding depends on the finder.**
:::

::: notes
And then people stopped arguing and counted. The Open Science Collaboration took a hundred psychology experiments and replicated them properly – high power, original materials, the original authors consulted where possible. Ninety-seven per cent of the original studies had reported a significant result. Thirty-six per cent of the replications did, and the effect sizes came back at about half the original size. That is the study that made 'replication crisis' a phrase outside methodology seminars. The second one is closest to home, because it is ours: seventy-three teams of sociologists and political scientists, one hypothesis about immigration and support for social policy, more than twelve hundred models between them, and no agreement on the sign, let alone the significance. Different fields, different designs, and the same uncomfortable conclusion. The finding depends on the finder.
:::

## It is not mostly fraud {.smaller}

::: {.small}
The mechanism is **ordinary and structural**:

- Journals reward novel, clean, significant results – so that is what gets written up
- Every analysis contains dozens of small defensible choices, and the analyst makes them while looking at the data
- Nobody publishes the twelve specifications that did not work; the reader sees one
- Data and code are usually not available, so nobody can check any of it
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Ask researchers anonymously, with an incentive to answer truthfully, and a **majority admit** to at least one of these practices – not fraud, the ordinary kind [@JohnEtAl2012MeasuringPrevalenceQuestionable]
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
None of these steps requires a dishonest person. That is exactly why the problem is hard: you cannot fix it by hiring better people.
:::

::: notes
Now the important qualification, and I want to be emphatic about it. This is not mostly a story about fraud. Fraud exists and it is spectacular when it surfaces, but it is rare and it is not what these numbers are measuring. The mechanism is ordinary and it is structural. Journals want novel, clean, significant results, so that is what gets submitted. Every analysis contains dozens of small, individually defensible choices, and the analyst makes them while looking at the data, because how else would you make them. Nobody writes up the twelve specifications that did not work, so the reader sees one path through a garden with hundreds. And in most cases neither the data nor the code are available, so nobody can check any of it. John, Loewenstein and Prelec went and asked researchers directly, anonymously, with a mechanism designed to make truthful answers worth giving – and a majority admitted to at least one of these practices. Not one of those steps requires a bad actor. Which is exactly why the problem is hard: you cannot solve it by hiring better people. [pause] So suppose you did hire the best people you could find, gave them all the same data and the same question, and watched. Somebody did exactly that.
:::

## Twenty-nine teams, one question {.smaller}

::: {.small}
**The question.** Are football referees more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players than to light-skinned ones?

**The data.** One dataset, sent to everyone: 2,053 players in the top divisions of England, Germany, France and Spain, the 3,147 referees they played under, and **146,028 player–referee pairs**. Skin tone rated from profile photographs by two coders who did not know the research question.

**The design.** Twenty-nine teams analysed it independently. They reviewed each other's approaches *before* anyone had seen a result, revised, and only then compared answers.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
This is the first many-analysts study. Every one since is a variation on it – including the one you are inside today.
:::

::: {.src}
@SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne
:::

::: notes
So let me show you the study that started all of this, because everything after it, including our own day, is a variation on its design. Silberzahn and colleagues, twenty eighteen. The question is deliberately concrete: are football referees more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players than to light-skinned ones? The data went to everyone identically – two thousand and fifty-three players in the top divisions of England, Germany, France and Spain, the three thousand referees they had played under, and a hundred and forty-six thousand player-referee pairs, with skin tone rated from profile photographs by two coders who were not told the research question. And then the part that makes it a study rather than a survey: twenty-nine teams analysed it independently, reviewed each other's approaches before anybody had seen a single result, revised, and only then compared answers. Nobody could tune their method to get a number they liked, because nobody knew what number anyone was getting.
:::

## All twenty-nine, side by side

```{r}
#| label: silberzahn-forest
#| fig-width: 9.6
#| fig-height: 5.0
# The paper's Figure 3, rebuilt from the authors' published values rather than
# reproduced as an image: every team, every interval, grouped by the response
# distribution it assumed. Colour is ours - the original is monochrome - and
# marks whether the interval excludes 1. Teams 21 and 27 have intervals running
# to 11.5 and 78.7; the published figure truncates both and asterisks them, and
# so does this.
CLIP <- 3.2
szf <- silberzahn29 |>
  mutate(hi_draw = pmin(or_hi, CLIP),
         lab = paste0(team, ". ", tidy_approach(approach))) |>
  arrange(distribution, or) |>
  mutate(lab = factor(lab, levels = rev(lab)))

ggplot(szf, aes(or, lab, colour = significant)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "longdash", colour = grey_mid) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = or_lo, xmax = hi_draw), height = 0, linewidth = 0.55) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  geom_text(data = filter(szf, or_hi > CLIP), aes(x = CLIP + 0.04, label = "*"),
            size = 5, vjust = 0.75, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = ncl_blue, `FALSE` = d_red),
                      breaks = c("TRUE", "FALSE"), name = NULL,
                      labels = c("interval excludes 1", "interval includes 1")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.03))) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.42, CLIP + 0.1)) +
  facet_grid(distribution ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  labs(x = "odds ratio", y = NULL,
       caption = paste("Above 1: dark-skinned players red-carded more often.",
                       "* interval runs past the edge (teams 21 and 27).")) +
  theme_slide(11) +
  theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 1, colour = "grey45", size = 9,
                                    margin = margin(t = 4)),
        legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "right",
        legend.margin = margin(0, 0, -6, 0),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 10, colour = "grey25"),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = "grey92"),
        strip.placement = "outside",
        strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, face = "bold",
                                         colour = ncl_blue, hjust = 1),
        axis.text.y = element_text(colour = "grey25", hjust = 0, size = 8.5),
        panel.spacing.y = unit(0.45, "lines"))
```

::: {.src}
@SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne, Figure 3, rebuilt from the published values at osf.io/gvm2z.
:::

::: notes
And here is what came back. Read it as a list of twenty-nine analyses of one dataset. The odds ratios run from nought point eight nine to two point nine three – the low end says dark-skinned players were red-carded slightly *less* often – and the median is one point three one. Twenty of the twenty-nine intervals exclude one; nine do not. So about two thirds found an effect and a third did not, on identical data. [pause] Now look at the left column, because that is where the day's real subject is. The teams are grouped by the response distribution they assumed – linear, logistic, Poisson, and two that fit none of the three. That is not a detail of implementation. It is a decision each team made, defensibly, before touching the data, and it is the same kind of decision you will be making after lunch. Hold on to that grouping; we come back to it twice.
:::

## 'Replication' crises

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Another 'replication' crisis – terminological confusion?
:::
::: {.fragment}
The term 'reproducibility' has been used as a synonym for a number of different characteristics – reproducibility, robustness, replicability, repeatability, credibility, and trustworthiness.
:::
[[Successfully rerun the same code on the same data?]{colour="#b22222"}]{.fragment}
[[Re-analyse the same data a different way?]{colour="#1C69A8"}]{.fragment}
[[Collect fresh data and analyse it in the same way?]{colour="#4D179A"}]{.fragment}
[[Using the same data and same analysis but asking a different question?]{colour="#3C6301"}]{.fragment}
[[Asking the same question but answering it with fresh data and a different analysis?]{colour="#3BB8DB"}]{.fragment}
::::

::: notes
So: twenty-nine competent teams, one dataset, and no agreement. Now notice what I have carefully not said yet – what *kind* of failure that is. And that turns out to be the whole difficulty, because part of the problem is the word itself. For years 'replication' covered everything: rerunning someone's code, re-analysing their data a different way, collecting new data altogether. Those are three different operations, answering three different questions – but because we called them all 'replication', the crisis debates had people talking past each other for a decade. So before any numbers, we need vocabulary.
:::

## The data $\times$ analysis matrix

```{r}
#| label: matrix
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 7
repeatability_matrix()
```

::: {.src}
@AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen; @NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms
:::

::: notes
Here is the whole framework on one slide, and if you take a single thing home today, make it this grid. The question stays the same throughout; what varies is the data and the analysis. Same data, same analysis – reproducibility: if I rerun your recipe, do I get your number? Same data but a different, justifiable analysis – robustness: does your finding survive my defensible choices? New data, same question – replicability. The fourth cell, new data and new analysis, is really generalisation, and we set it aside today. Sit with this for a moment – everything that follows this morning hangs off it.
:::

## Credibility is not truth

::: {.scaled style="--fs: 0.9; --lh: 1.15"}
**Repeatability** is used when referring to reproducibility, robustness, and replicability as a constellation of concepts intended to assess whether answers to scientific questions are unchanged when different steps of the research process are repeated.

**Credibility** and **trustworthiness** refer to the confidence one can have in research findings. Because scientific knowledge claims are tentative, they are *not* synonymous with truth.

For example, credibility is advanced by addressing potential competing interests in the conducting and reporting of research, by taking existing knowledge into account, by using methods that have been validated, by controlling for biases in the research context, by pursuing precise and reliable evidence, and by calibrating the strength of the claims to the uncertainty of the evidence.
:::

::: {.src}
@NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms
:::

::: notes
The glossary is worth reading slowly, because it separates two things we routinely run together. Repeatability is the umbrella: reproducibility, robustness and replicability as a family, all asking whether the answer survives repeating some step of the process. Credibility and trustworthiness are about how much confidence a finding deserves – and note the sentence in the middle. Because scientific claims are tentative, credibility is not the same as truth. A credible finding can be wrong. What credibility is built from is the list at the bottom: declared interests, validated methods, precise evidence, and claims calibrated to the uncertainty behind them. That last one is the one we will keep coming back to.
:::

## Open research: the practices {.smaller}

::: {.small}
| Practice | What it makes possible |
|---|---|
| **Open data** | Someone else can re-analyse your evidence |
| **Open code** | Someone else can rerun your exact analysis |
| **Open materials** | Someone else can run your study again |
| **Open access** | Someone else can read the claim in the first place |
| **Preregistration** | A dated record of the plan, before the results exist |
| **Registered reports** | Peer review of the plan, with publication decided before results |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Each one removes a specific obstacle. None of them is a general-purpose guarantee. The programme, set out at length: [@MunafoEtAl2017ManifestoReproducibleScience]
:::

::: notes
So what does open research actually propose? Not a philosophy – a list of practices, and each one removes a specific, identifiable obstacle. Open data means someone else can re-analyse your evidence rather than taking your word for it. Open code means they can rerun your exact analysis. Open materials means they can run the study again in a new sample. Open access means they can read the thing at all, which sounds trivial until you try to get a paper from outside a wealthy university. Preregistration produces a dated record of the plan before the results exist. And registered reports go further: the plan is peer-reviewed and the publication decision is made before anyone sees a result, which removes the incentive to find something. Each removes one obstacle. None is a general guarantee, and I want to be clear about that before we get enthusiastic.
:::

## What openness does not fix {.smaller}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
A fully open, perfectly reproducible pipeline can still answer **the wrong question**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
It can still be built on a **selected sample**, a **mismeasured** construct, or an **untestable assumption**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
> "Reproducibility success does not mean that the finding is correct." [@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial]
:::

::: {.fragment}
Openness makes claims **checkable**. It does not make them **right**. The checking is still work, and someone still has to do it.
:::
::::

::: notes
Here is the qualification that the enthusiasm usually skips. A completely open, perfectly reproducible pipeline can still be answering the wrong question. It can still rest on a selected sample, or a construct that does not measure what its name says, or an assumption nobody can test. The sentence on the slide is from one of the papers we are about to meet, and it deserves a beat of silence: reproducibility success does not mean the finding is correct. All openness does – and this is still a great deal – is make claims checkable. It does not make them right. Somebody still has to do the checking, and that turns out to be the interesting part, because when people do the checking at scale you get the three studies we look at next.
:::

## What is SCORE?

::: {.small}
- DARPA-funded programme to gauge the credibility of social-science claims
- **62 journals**, papers from **2009–2018**, stratified sample
- Each paper's central claim traced from abstract to the supporting statistic
- Thousands of researchers; three repetition studies built on the same frame
:::

::: notes
Where do these numbers come from? All three papers sit on one programme, SCORE – funded by DARPA, oddly enough, who wanted to know whether you could predict which findings hold up. The backbone is a stratified sample from sixty-two journals, papers published between 2009 and 2018, with each paper's central claim traced from the abstract down to the exact statistic that supports it. The three studies then took that same frame and each asked one of our three questions. So when the numbers land in a moment, they are about the same body of literature, asked three different things.
:::

## Reproducibility – Miske et al.

::: {.small}
- **600 papers** sampled (62 journals, 2009–2018)
- Ask the authors for data and code, then try to rerun the reported result
- How often can we even get to the starting line?
:::

::: {.src}
@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial.
:::

::: notes
First, reproducibility – the gentlest test of the three. The design in one breath: take six hundred papers, ask the authors for their data and code, and try to recompute the central reported result. Same data, same analysis: do you get the same number? Before we even ask how often that works, the first finding is about how rarely you can even start.
:::

## Most papers never reach the starting line

```{r}
#| label: miske-waterfall
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
# Waterfall from 600 sampled -> 143 assessable, inline data from the content
# bank (Miske et al. 2026). Illustrative staged counts, clearly labelled.
mw <- tibble::tribble(
  ~stage,                 ~n,
  "Sampled",              600,
  "Data available\n(24.0%)", 144,
  "Assessable",           143
)
mw <- mw |> dplyr::mutate(stage = factor(stage, levels = stage))
ggplot(mw, aes(stage, n, fill = stage)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.4, fontface = "bold",
            colour = ncl_blue, size = 6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(ncl_blue, orange, green)) +
  ylim(0, 660) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "papers") +
  theme_slide(16)
```

::: {.small}
- Of the **143 assessable**: **53.6%** reproduced precisely, **73.5%** approximately
- Counting the unassessable, only about **18%** reproduce
:::

::: notes
Read it left to right. Six hundred papers sampled. Data were available for twenty-four per cent of them – for nearly three quarters there was neither data nor code. That leaves 143 papers you can actually assess. Of those, just over half reproduce precisely, and about three quarters at least approximately. Which sounds respectable – until you notice what happens if you count the papers nobody could check as failures: the overall rate falls to roughly eighteen per cent. The barrier is not arithmetic. It is access.
:::

## Why some fields do better

::: {.small}
- Journals requiring data sharing: **87.5–100%** availability vs **16.0%** without
- Political science **54.1%** data availability vs education **2.9%**
- With data *and* code: **90.9%** approx-reproducible vs **38.1%** from rebuilt source
:::

::: {.claimcard}
"The most substantial barrier … was the unavailability of author data."

"Reproducibility success does not mean that the finding is correct."
:::

::: {.src}
@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial.
:::

::: notes
And access follows policy. Where journals mandate data sharing, availability sits between about ninety and one hundred per cent; without a mandate, sixteen. Political science and economics built the habit early and are far ahead of the rest. The first quote is the paper's own conclusion – the biggest barrier was simply that the data were not there. The second quote deserves a beat of silence: "reproducibility success does not mean that the finding is correct." Reproducing a number tells you the computation was faithful. It does not tell you the claim about the world is true.
:::

## Robustness – Aczel et al. (Multi100)

::: {.small}
- **100 studies**, each re-analysed by **≥5 independent analysts**
- Same data; each analyst free to choose any *justifiable* analysis
- A peer panel judges whether each pipeline is appropriate
- I was one of its analysts
:::

::: {.src}
@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness.
:::

::: notes
The middle paper – the one I was in. One hundred studies, and for each one at least five analysts working independently: no teams, original authors barred, everyone handed the same data and the same claim. You were free to analyse it any way you could justify, and a peer panel later judged whether your pipeline was appropriate. Two things worth knowing about the design. The hundred studies had already passed a reproducibility check – so robustness was being measured on the reproducible subset, the best-case material. And we were not blinded: every analyst saw the full original article, published estimates and all, so if anything we were anchored towards the original answer.
:::

## Same data, five analysts, different answers

::: {.small}
- **34%** of reanalysis effect sizes within ±0.05 *d* of the original (57% within ±0.20)
- **74%** reached the same conclusion; 24% null/inconclusive; **2%** opposite
- Effect sizes shrank: original mean *d* **0.73** → reanalysis **0.49**
- Analyst-to-analyst variability typically **exceeds** sampling error
:::

::: {.src}
@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness.
:::

::: notes
So what do free, justifiable choices do to the same data? They move the answer – a lot. Only about a third of the reanalyses landed within five hundredths of a Cohen's d of the original, and in just five studies out of ninety-five did all the analysts land that close. Conclusions held up better than magnitudes: three quarters of reanalyses agreed with the original conclusion. But the effect sizes shrank, from a mean d of point seven three down to point four nine. And the finding I keep coming back to: the spread across analysts is typically larger than the statistical uncertainty inside any single analysis. The analyst, in other words, is a bigger source of noise than the sample. One more detail to hold for later: observational studies – which is what we work on today – came out less robust than experiments.
:::

## Replicability – Tyner et al.

::: {.small}
- **274 claims** from 164 papers, tested on **new data**
- Median statistical power **99.6%**; preregistered; original authors consulted
- The strictest test: does the effect reappear in a fresh sample?
:::

::: {.src}
@TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial.
:::

::: notes
The third paper is the strictest test: not the same data analysed differently, but genuinely new data. Two hundred and seventy-four claims, each replicated to a preregistered, peer-reviewed protocol, often with the original authors consulted, and with a median statistical power of ninety-nine point six per cent. That last number matters: these studies were built so that a real effect would be very hard to miss. So whatever fails here is not failing for lack of trying.
:::

## Even success shrinks

```{r}
#| label: tyner-shrink
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.2
# Median r: original -> replication (Tyner et al. 2026), inline dumbbell.
sh <- tibble::tibble(
  stage = factor(c("Original", "Replication"),
                 levels = c("Original", "Replication")),
  r = c(0.25, 0.10)
)
ggplot(sh, aes(r, y = 1)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = 1), colour = grey_mid, linewidth = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = stage), size = 8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", r)), vjust = -1.6,
            fontface = "bold", colour = ncl_blue, size = 6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = stage), vjust = 3.2, colour = ncl_blue, size = 5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(ncl_blue, orange)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.3)) +
  labs(x = "median effect size (r)", y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(16) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

::: {.small}
- **55.1%** of claims replicated by significance; effect sizes roughly **halve**
- Thirteen success criteria give anywhere from **29%** to **75%**
:::

::: {.src}
@TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial.
:::

::: notes
And this is what comes back. The median effect size halves: point two five in the originals, point one zero in the replications. By the significance criterion, fifty-five per cent of claims replicate. But notice that "did it replicate?" is not even one question – the team scored the same studies against thirteen reasonable success criteria and got answers ranging from twenty-nine to seventy-five per cent. Two sentences from the paper are worth carrying around. "Strictly speaking, there is no such thing as exact replication." And: "The problem to solve is not unreplicability per se, it is overconfidence."
:::

## The three Rs do not travel together

:::: {.none}
Reproducible ≠ robust ≠ replicable.

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
Across SCORE the three are [**essentially uncorrelated**]{.highlight bg-colour="#ffe3b3"} – knowing one barely predicts the others.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
So there is no single number for 'trust'. You have to ask *which* repetition you mean.
:::
::::

::: notes
Now the bit that genuinely surprised me. You would hope these three properties travel together – that a reproducible finding is more likely to be robust, and a robust one more likely to replicate. Across SCORE, they do not. Measured on the same body of papers, the three indicators are essentially uncorrelated – knowing one tells you almost nothing about the others. So there is no single trust score for a finding. "Is it reliable?" is an incomplete question until you say which kind of repetition you mean. Hold that thought, because we are about to watch all three play out on one single paper.
:::

## Quick check: credibility in the wild {.questionslide transition="fade-in none-out"}

::: {.none}
You submit your paper and replication package. It goes out to reviewers.

- "Reviewer 1" wants to ensure that your results are [reproducible]{.fragment .bounceIn}, so she sources your R script to run the entire analysis. You're in luck – she hasn't yet updated her `dplyr`, so the code runs.
- "Reviewer 2" is very eager. He's unconvinced by your modelling choices, so he fits your data to another function to check if your findings are truly [robust]{.fragment .bounceIn}. You're in luck again – he recovers your point estimate to a reasonable precision, although the confidence intervals have widened.
- "Reviewer 3" takes a special interest because he's just working on a similar paper on data they published recently. Do your results [replicate]{.fragment .bounceIn} when your methods are applied to that state-of-the-art dataset?
:::

## Quick check: credibility in the wild {.questionslide transition="none-in fade-out"}

::: {.none}
You submit your paper and replication package. It goes out to reviewers.

"Reviewer 2" just doesn't want to let go...

- He tried a few alternative analyses of your data, including a fancy new regression method that he just released as an R package. His method gives results that are generally aligned to yours, but for the method to work, it would require a larger dataset; would your results really [generalise]{.fragment .bounceIn} to this new dataset published by "Reviewer 3" that he just read about, if applying his new fancy method to it?
:::


## Inside Multi100: what an analyst was sent {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- A **published paper**, in full – no blinding: I could see the original estimates
- Its **central claim**, in one sentence, lifted from the abstract
- A pointer to the **data** – in our case, sixteen Eurobarometer waves you fetch yourself from GESIS
- No instructions on method. Analyse it any way you can defend
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
And two things I could not see: **who the other analysts were**, and **what they were finding**.
:::

::: {.src}
@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness. Registered protocol: osf.io/7snkz
:::

::: notes
Let me show you what this was like from the inside, because it shapes how you read the results. What arrived was a published paper – the whole thing, not blinded, so I could see the original estimates, and if anything that anchors you towards the original answer. With it came the paper's central claim in a single sentence, lifted from the abstract, and a pointer to where the data lived. In our case that meant sixteen Eurobarometer waves that I had to go and fetch from GESIS myself, under licence. What did not arrive was any instruction on method. Analyse it however you can defend. And two things stayed hidden throughout: who the other analysts were, and what any of them were finding. That isolation is the design – it is what makes the spread at the end mean something.
:::

## The paper, for now in one slide

::: {.small}
- Author: I will say **OA**, the original author, from here on
- **Does the EU economic crisis undermine support for the EU?** – 16 Eurobarometer waves, **2004–2013**, about **390,000** respondents in **27 countries**

::: {.claimcard}
"The results show, first, that *poor economic performances* **increase negative** and **decrease positive** *dimensions of EU framing*."
:::

- Macro predictors: **national unemployment** and **GDP growth**. Outcome: what people say the EU means to them, sorted into four framing scales
:::

::: {.src}
@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic. The full methodological reading is Part 2.
:::

::: notes
And here is the paper, briefly – we spend most of Part 2 inside it, so this is just enough to follow what happened. It is from 2016, in the European Sociological Review, and I will call its author OA, the original author, throughout the day. The question is whether the economic crisis undermined how people relate to the EU: sixteen Eurobarometer waves from 2004 to 2013, the crisis decade, about three hundred and ninety thousand respondents across twenty-seven member states. The claim we were handed is the sentence in the box. On the right-hand side sit two macro indicators, national unemployment and GDP growth; on the left, what people say the EU means to them personally, sorted into four framing scales. That is all you need for now. Part 2 opens by taking the whole thing apart.
:::

## Two tasks, months apart {.smaller}

::: {.small}
**Task 1 – free reanalysis.** Reanalyse the claim however you see fit. Record one categorical conclusion: does the evidence support it?

::: {.fragment}
**Task 2 – constrained reanalysis.** Months later, three instructions arrive that fix the question:

- use the **cosmopolitan** framing dimension as the outcome
- use the **unemployment rate** as the predictor
- **disregard** the contextual variables
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Task 1 measures whether we agree. Task 2 makes our *numbers* comparable – you cannot average five answers to five different questions.
:::

::: notes
The study ran in two stages, and the distinction matters for everything that follows. Task one was complete freedom: reanalyse the claim however you see fit, and record one categorical conclusion – does the evidence support it or not. Then months later, task two arrived with three instructions that pinned the question down: use the cosmopolitan framing dimension as your outcome, use the unemployment rate as your predictor, and disregard the contextual variables. Now, why run it in that order? Because the two tasks measure different things. Task one asks whether independent analysts reach the same verdict. Task two asks whether they produce the same number – and you can only ask that second question once everyone is answering the same question, which is precisely what those three instructions manufacture.
:::

## How a hundred studies become one number {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- Every analyst reports their test statistic and its degrees of freedom, in whatever form their model produces – **t**, **z**, **F**, χ²
- Each is converted to a **partial correlation** *r* and a standardised **Cohen's *d***, so a Stata pooled model and an R multilevel model land on the same axis
- A **peer panel** judges whether each pipeline is an appropriate analysis of the claim
- Only then can you ask: how far apart are five defensible answers?
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Standardising is what makes comparison possible – and it quietly assumes the five are estimating **the same quantity**. Hold that thought until Part 2.
:::

::: notes
So how do you compare a hundred studies analysed five ways each? Everyone reports the test statistic their model happens to produce, with its degrees of freedom – a t, a z, an F, a chi-squared. Those get converted onto a common scale: a partial correlation and a standardised mean difference, so that somebody's pooled Stata model and somebody else's R multilevel model can sit on the same axis and be read against each other. Alongside that, a peer panel judged whether each pipeline was an appropriate analysis of the claim at all – so the spread you are about to see is a spread among analyses that passed review, not a spread that includes nonsense. And notice the assumption hiding in the conversion: putting five numbers on one axis takes for granted that they estimate the same quantity. Hold on to that. Part 2 is largely about what happens when they do not.
:::


## Our five: one sign, very different sizes {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: forest5
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 4.1
# Five Multi100 analysts of the SAME claim, from ../data/analysts5.csv.
# Standardised partial r on one axis; C6HJR highlighted. The label carries the
# software and the document format, because this chart is also the bridge into
# the tools segment: the spread is not caused by the toolchain, but the fact
# that every analyst shipped a readable, runnable document is what made the
# spread diagnosable afterwards.
fa <- analysts5 |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    me  = analyst_id == "C6HJR",
    lab = paste0(analyst_id, "   ", tool, "  ", document)
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(r) |>
  dplyr::mutate(lab = factor(lab, levels = lab))

ggplot(fa, aes(r, lab, colour = me)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = grey_mid, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(size = 6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("r = %.2f", r)),
            hjust = -0.25, size = 4.5, colour = ncl_blue) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = ncl_blue, `TRUE` = orange)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.55, 0.10)) +
  labs(x = "partial correlation r (same claim, same data, five analysts)",
       y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(15)
```

::: {.small}
- All five negative – same direction · partial *r* from **−0.45 to −0.006** · one not significant
:::

::: {.src}
Task 2 results as recorded in the public Multi100 dataset (osf.io/q5h2c).
:::

::: notes
And here are the five of us, on this one claim. All five found a negative effect – on direction, unanimity. On size, look at the spread: from essentially zero, and that one is not significant, out to a partial correlation of minus point four five. Two orders of magnitude apart, on the same data, for the same claim, with all three of Task 2's instructions obeyed. The orange dot is me, at minus point two four. Five competent people, one fixed question, and the answers scatter across half the available range. Now – before we go anywhere near why, which is Part 2's whole job, I want you to look at the labels down the left-hand side, because there is a column there I have not mentioned yet.
:::

## Look at the labels {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- Two of us worked in **Stata**, three in **R**
- Within R, three different document formats: a plain `.R` script, an `.Rmd`, a `.qmd`
:::

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
The software did **not** cause the spread. There is no Stata answer and R answer to this claim.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
But because each of us submitted a document somebody else could **open and run**, it became possible, afterwards, to find out what *did* cause it.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
That is the whole case for the toolchain – and it is what you spend this afternoon doing.
:::
::::

::: notes
Two of the five worked in Stata, three in R – and within R, three different document formats: a plain script, an R Markdown file, a Quarto file. Now, the tempting reading of that column is the wrong one, so let me kill it straight away. The software did not cause the spread. There is no Stata answer and no R answer to this claim; every one of these models can be fitted in either. But here is what the column does tell you, and it is the entire case for caring about tooling. Because every one of us submitted a document that somebody else could open and run, it became possible afterwards to go and find out what actually did cause the spread. I have read all four of the others' code, line by line, and this afternoon you will work inside the same space they were working in. That is only possible because of what is in that column. So – the tools.
:::

## What open source buys you {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- **You can read it.** The estimator is not a black box you are asked to trust – the source of `lm()`, of `feols()`, of every package we load today, is public
- **No licence stands between a reader and your analysis.** Anyone, anywhere, can run your code without buying anything
- **It outlives your institution.** A licence expires when you change job; a package on CRAN does not
- **You can fix it, and so can others.** Bugs get found because thousands of people run the same code on different data
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The point is not free-as-in-beer. It is that **reproducibility has a price**, and a proprietary toolchain quietly puts that price on your reader.
:::

::: notes
Why does open source matter here specifically? Four reasons, and only one of them is money. First, you can read it: the estimator is not a black box you are asked to trust – you can go and look at the source of any function we run today. Second, and this is the one that bears on our subject, no licence stands between a reader and your analysis. If your replication package needs a licence they do not have, your work is not reproducible for them, however carefully you wrote it. Third, it outlives your institution – a site licence ends when you change job, and a package on CRAN does not. Fourth, bugs get found, because thousands of people run the same code against different data. The point is not free as in beer. It is that reproducibility has a price, and a proprietary toolchain quietly hands that price to your reader.
:::

## The toolchain, laid out {.smaller}

::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 4"}
<div class="grouphead">Analyse</div>
<div class="tool ours"><img src="pics/tools/r.svg" alt="R"><span class="name">R</span><span class="what">statistics-first language</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/python.png" alt="Python"><span class="name">Python</span><span class="what">general purpose, strong ML</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/julia.png" alt="Julia"><span class="name">Julia</span><span class="what">fast numerics</span></div>

Here is the whole landscape on one slide, in three jobs rather than three brand families. First, something to analyse with – R, which is what we use, but Python and Julia are entirely reasonable homes for this work, and Stata and SPSS are still the default in a lot of departments. Third, the part people skip: publishing and sharing. Quarto turns text and code into a document; git records every version with a date; GitHub is where the repository lives so others can reach it; and OSF or Zenodo give the whole thing a permanent address with a DOI. Ringed in orange is what today runs on. The rest is the map.

## Languages: what you are actually choosing {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 4"}
<div class="tool ours"><img src="pics/tools/r.svg" alt="R"><span class="name">R</span><span class="what">Built by statisticians for data analysis. Unbeatable for models, tables and figures; the ecosystem is the reason.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/python.png" alt="Python"><span class="name">Python</span><span class="what">A general language that also does data. Better for pipelines, scraping, text and machine learning.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/julia.png" alt="Julia"><span class="name">Julia</span><span class="what">Fast, young, small ecosystem. Worth it when your model takes hours.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/stata.svg" alt="Stata"><span class="name">Stata</span><span class="what">Excellent panel and survey estimators, superb docs, one syntax. Costs money and hides its source.</span></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
You do not have to choose once and forever. Quarto runs R, Python and Julia chunks in the **same document**, and today's browser lab is R compiled to run inside a web page.
:::

::: notes
A slower look at the languages, because people agonise about this and mostly should not. R was built by statisticians for data analysis, and that is still where it wins – models, tables, figures, and above all the ecosystem: whatever obscure estimator your literature uses, someone has written the package. Python is a general-purpose language that also does data, so it is the better home for pipelines, scraping, text and machine learning. Julia is fast and young with a small ecosystem, and earns its place when a model takes hours rather than seconds. Stata deserves respect – genuinely excellent panel and survey estimators, the best documentation in the business, one consistent syntax – and it costs money and hides its source. The reassuring part is that this is not a life choice. Quarto will run R, Python and Julia chunks in the same document.
:::

## Plain text is the format that survives {.smaller}

::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 4"}
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/terminal.png" alt="R script"><span class="name">.R</span><span class="what">Code only. Comments carry the prose.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/markdown.png" alt="Markdown"><span class="name">.md</span><span class="what">Prose only. Headings, lists, links – no code.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/rmarkdown.png" alt="R Markdown"><span class="name">.Rmd</span><span class="what">Prose + R, rendered together. R only.</span></div>
<div class="tool ours"><img src="pics/tools/quarto.png" alt="Quarto"><span class="name">.qmd</span><span class="what">Prose + R, Python or Julia. Today's format.</span></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Every one of these is a **plain text file**. You can open it in anything, diff it, email it, and read it in twenty years. A `.docx` with pasted output is none of those things – and it has no idea which numbers came from which code.
:::

::: notes
This is the slide I would keep if I could keep only one from this segment. Four file types, in increasing order of what they hold. A dot-R file is code with comments. A markdown file is prose with no code. An R Markdown file is prose and R together, rendered into one document. And a Quarto file is the same idea, except the code can be R or Python or Julia. What they have in common is the thing that matters: every one is a plain text file. You can open it in any editor, see exactly what changed between two versions, email it, and still read it in twenty years. Compare that with a Word document holding numbers you pasted in from somewhere. It looks the same on the page, and it has no idea which number came from which line of code. That gap is where errors live.
:::

## How a document becomes a document

![](pics/tools/render-pipeline.png){fig-align="center" width="72%"}

::: {.small}
You write **one** source file. The rendering step runs your code, drops the results in, and produces whatever output you asked for – all from the same source.
:::

::: notes
And this is what happens when you press render. You write one source file: prose and code together. Knitr – or Jupyter, if you are working in Python – runs every chunk of code in a fresh session and replaces it with its actual output, giving a plain markdown file. Pandoc then turns that into whatever you asked for: a Word document for your co-author, a PDF for the journal, a web page for your project site, slides like these. Notice what this buys you. There is exactly one place where a number is computed, and every output carries the same number, because they were all produced from the same source in the same run. When a reviewer asks you to drop three countries, you change one line and re-render, and the table, the figure and the sentence in the text all move together. That is worth learning for its own sake, quite apart from anything about credibility.
:::

## The package layer {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 4"}
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/pkg-tidyverse.png" alt="tidyverse"><span class="name">tidyverse</span><span class="what">Reading, reshaping, plotting. One grammar across all of it.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/pkg-easystats.png" alt="easystats"><span class="name">easystats</span><span class="what">Model output as tidy data: parameters, performance, effect sizes.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/pkg-modelsummary.png" alt="modelsummary"><span class="name">modelsummary</span><span class="what">Regression tables you can publish, from the fitted objects.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/pkg-marginaleffects.png" alt="marginaleffects"><span class="name">marginaleffects</span><span class="what">Predictions, contrasts and marginal effects from almost any model.</span></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Today also loads **`fixest`** (fast fixed effects – the estimator behind our baseline), **`dagitty`** and **`ggdag`** (causal graphs). The full setup is on the setup page; the browser lab has it all preloaded.
:::

::: notes
A word about packages, because this is where R's advantage actually sits. The tidyverse gives you one consistent grammar for reading data, reshaping it and plotting it, so once you have learned the verbs they work everywhere. Easystats turns model output back into tidy data – coefficients, fit statistics, effect sizes – instead of the printed blob that summary gives you. Modelsummary builds publication-ready regression tables straight from fitted model objects, so your table cannot disagree with your model. And marginaleffects computes predictions, contrasts and marginal effects from almost any model you can fit, which is how you get from a coefficient to a statement in the units your reader thinks in. Today we also use fixest for fast fixed effects – that is the estimator behind our baseline – and dagitty and ggdag for the causal graphs. Route 2 people have all of it already.
:::

## Version control, in one slide {.smaller .deepdive}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**Git** is a program on your machine. It records a **complete, dated snapshot** every time you say so, and it never forgets one.

**GitHub** is a website that hosts those snapshots so other people can reach them – and it is not the only one (GitLab, Codeberg, your university's own).
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
What it gives you that a folder of `final_v3_REALLY_final.R` cannot:

- Every past state, recoverable exactly
- A written reason attached to each change
- A public, timestamped trail of when you knew what
- A way for two people to edit the same file without one overwriting the other
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
We use **none of it today** – deliberately. There is a companion module on the site, and your workspace folder is the ideal thing to practise on.
:::

::: notes
Version control is the tool I have deliberately kept out of today, so let me at least name it properly. Git is a program that runs on your machine: every time you tell it to, it records a complete dated snapshot of your project, and it never forgets one. GitHub is a website that hosts those snapshots so other people can reach them – and it is worth knowing that GitHub is not the only one, there is GitLab, there is Codeberg, and your university may run its own. What does that give you that a folder full of final-version-three-really-final does not? Every past state recoverable exactly, a written reason attached to every change, a public timestamped trail of when you knew what – which, notice, is a preregistration mechanism in itself – and a way for two people to work on one file without one silently overwriting the other. There is a companion module on the site.
:::

## Where data and code go to live {.smaller}

::: {.toolgrid style="--cols: 4"}
<div class="tool ours"><img src="pics/tools/osf.png" alt="OSF"><span class="name">OSF</span><span class="what">Projects, files, and registrations. Free, and where our case's trail lives.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/zenodo.svg" alt="Zenodo"><span class="name">Zenodo</span><span class="what">CERN-run archive. Gives a DOI; takes a GitHub release directly.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><img src="pics/tools/dataverse.svg" alt="Dataverse"><span class="name">Dataverse</span><span class="what">Institutional data archives with proper metadata and curation.</span></div>
<div class="tool"><span class="badge" style="--tint:#4a6741">XYZ</span><span class="name">Your domain's archive</span><span class="what">GESIS, UK Data Service, ICPSR – licensed access to survey microdata.</span></div>
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
**A repository is not an archive.** GitHub can be force-pushed, renamed, or deleted tomorrow. An archived deposit gets a **DOI**, a fixed version, and a commitment to keep serving it. Serious work usually needs both.
:::

::: notes
And the last group: where things go so they are still there in ten years. OSF is free, holds projects and files and registrations, and it is where our case's whole public trail lives – you will be reading it after lunch. Zenodo is run by CERN, gives you a DOI, and will take a GitHub release directly, which makes archiving a one-click habit. Dataverse is the institutional data-archive world with proper metadata and curation. And then the domain archives – GESIS, the UK Data Service, ICPSR – which is where licensed survey microdata lives, including the Eurobarometer data behind our paper. Now the distinction people get wrong, and it is on the slide. A repository is not an archive. A GitHub repository can be force-pushed, renamed or deleted tomorrow, and the link in your paper dies. An archived deposit has a DOI, a fixed version and an institution committed to serving it. Serious work usually needs both.
:::

## Licences, briefly {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.small}
| What | Common choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Code** | MIT · GPL | MIT: use it however you like. GPL: and share your changes back |
| **Data** | CC0 · CC BY | CC0 puts it in the public domain; CC BY asks for attribution |
| **Text, figures, slides** | CC BY · CC BY-NC | Attribution, optionally no commercial reuse |
| **Someone else's data** | *their* terms | Eurobarometer is GESIS-licensed – I may not redistribute it, and neither may you |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
"No licence" is not a neutral default. It means **all rights reserved** – legally, nobody may reuse it at all.
:::

::: notes
Licensing gets skipped and then bites. Four rows. For code, MIT says use it however you like, GPL says use it and share your changes back. For data, CC-zero puts it in the public domain and CC-BY asks for attribution. For text and figures and slides, CC-BY or CC-BY with a non-commercial clause. And the fourth row is the one that constrains our day: when the data are not yours, their terms govern. The Eurobarometer microdata behind our paper is GESIS-licensed – I am not allowed to redistribute it, which is why you will be working on an aggregate I built and am allowed to share, and it is also, as you will see, the reason the original reproduction attempt on this paper ran into trouble. And the line at the bottom: putting no licence on your repository is not generosity. Legally it means all rights reserved, so nobody may reuse it at all.
:::

## What the tools cannot do {.smaller}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
A perfectly reproducible pipeline can be a perfectly reproducible answer to **a question you never stated**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
None of this software will tell you what your estimand is, whether your controls belong in the model, or whether the association you found means what you think it means.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Tooling is the **cheap** half of the problem. We have now done it. **The rest of the day is the expensive half.**
:::
::::

::: notes
And I want to end this segment by undercutting it slightly. Everything I have just shown you is genuinely worth having – but a perfectly reproducible pipeline can be a perfectly reproducible answer to a question you never stated. None of this software will tell you what your estimand is. None of it will tell you whether the variables you put in the model belong there. None of it will tell you whether the association you found means what you think it means. Tooling is the cheap half of the problem, in the sense that it is solvable by learning things – which is what we have just done. The rest of the day is the expensive half, and it starts after the break with the most useful question in quantitative research, which is: what exactly are you trying to estimate?
:::

# PART 2 – The question underneath {.darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 2 · 90 minutes
:::

::: notes
Part two. We left the morning with five analysts, one claim, and answers spanning two orders of magnitude. This part answers why. It begins by going properly inside the paper – what it actually claimed, what it actually fitted, and what happened when three different kinds of repetition were tried on it. Then it turns the question around: a great deal of what gets called analysis variability turns out to be *question* variability, and analysts who look like they disagree about an answer are very often answering different questions without noticing. So we build the two tools that let you say precisely which question you are asking – the estimand, and the causal graph – and you use both before lunch.
:::
## The paper we spend the day inside

::: {.small}
- 16 Eurobarometer waves, **2004–2013**; about **390,000** respondents in **27 countries**

::: {.claimcard}
"The results show, first, that *poor economic performances* **increase negative** and **decrease positive** *dimensions of EU framing*."
:::

- "What does the EU mean to you personally?"
  - COSMOPOLITAN: positive non-materialist form of EU framing ('Peace'; 'Democracy'; 'Freedom to travel, study and work anywhere in the EU'; 'Cultural diversity'; 'Stronger say in the world')
  - UTILITARIAN: positive materialist form of EU framing (economic prosperity and social protection)
  - COMMUNITARIAN: negative non-materialist form of EU framing ('Loss of our cultural identity'; 'More crime'; 'Not enough control at external borders'; 'Unemployment')
  - LIBERTARIAN: negative materialist form of EU framing ('Bureaucracy'; 'Waste of money')
:::
::: {.src}
@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic.
:::
::: notes
Back to OA's paper, and this time properly. Sixteen Eurobarometer waves, 2004 to 2013 – the crisis decade – about three hundred and ninety thousand respondents across twenty-seven member states. The outcome comes from one rather good survey item: what does the EU mean to you personally? Thirteen response options, which OA organises into four framing scales, and read those slowly because the whole afternoon turns on them. Cosmopolitan is the positive non-materialist one: peace, democracy, freedom to travel and study and work anywhere, cultural diversity, a stronger voice in the world. Utilitarian is positive and materialist: prosperity and social protection. Communitarian and libertarian are the negative pair. That sorting into four scales is itself a substantive theoretical claim about what the EU means to people, and it is one you could argue with – which, this afternoon, several of you will.
:::

## The claim card, as analysts received it

::: {.claimcard}
"… poor economic performances … decrease positive dimensions of EU framing"

<span class="src">Teney (2016: 619)</span>
:::

::: {.small}
- Anchor result – unemployment → cosmopolitan framing, Table 3 Model 1:
- **b = −0.00340 · [t = −4.03]{.highlight bg-colour="#ffe3b3"} · p < .001**
:::

::: notes
This is, word for word, the claim every Multi100 analyst was handed: "poor economic performances decrease positive dimensions of EU framing". And this is the anchor number behind it, from Table 3, Model 1 – the unemployment coefficient on cosmopolitan framing: minus point zero zero three four, t of minus four. Keep one wrinkle in mind for later. In the paper's own Model 2, with more controls in, that same coefficient drops by more than half and loses significance. The robustness question is already alive inside the original paper.
:::


## What OA actually fitted {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- The unit is a **person**, not a country-year: roughly 390,000 respondents
- Thirteen response options collapse into **four framing scales** – cosmopolitan, utilitarian, communitarian, libertarian
- A **three-level** model: respondents inside country-waves inside countries
- Individual covariates: sex · age · education band · occupational status · urbanisation · left–right placement
- Macro predictors: **unemployment rate** and **GDP growth**, entering at the country-wave level
- Plus **cross-level interactions** – does the macro effect differ by education?
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Anchor result, Table 3 Model 1 – unemployment on cosmopolitan framing: **b = −0.00340 · t = −4.03 · p < .001**
:::

::: {.src}
@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic.
:::

::: notes
So what is under the bonnet? The unit of analysis is a person – around three hundred and ninety thousand of them – not a country-year. The outcome comes from a single survey item with thirteen response options, which OA collapses into four framing scales: cosmopolitan, utilitarian, communitarian, libertarian. The model is three-level: respondents inside country-waves inside countries. At the individual level there are the usual controls – sex, age, education band, occupational status, urbanisation, left-right placement. The two macro predictors, unemployment and GDP growth, enter at the country-wave level. And there are cross-level interactions, asking whether the macro effect differs by education. The anchor number for our claim, from Table 3 Model 1, is the unemployment coefficient on cosmopolitan framing: minus point zero zero three four, t of minus four.
:::

## The robustness question is already in the paper {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- **Model 1**: unemployment → cosmopolitan framing · b = −0.00340 · t = −4.03 · p < .001
- **Model 2**: the same coefficient, with further controls added – drops by more than half and **loses significance**
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Two models, one paper, and the claim's support depends on which one you read. The paper reports both, which is more than many do.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Notice what this means for today: the sixth analyst's problem – *which defensible specification do I report?* – was **already live inside the original study**, before any of us arrived.
:::

::: notes
And here is something worth pausing on, because it is easy to miss and it reframes the whole exercise. Look at what happens inside OA's own paper. Model one gives the anchor result: minus point zero zero three four, t of minus four, comfortably significant. Model two, which adds further controls, takes that same coefficient, more than halves it, and loses significance. Two models, one paper, and whether the claim is supported depends on which of them you read. To be fair to OA, the paper reports both – which is more than a great many papers do. But notice what it means for us. The problem you will face this afternoon, as the sixth analyst – which of several defensible specifications do I report, and on what grounds? – was already live inside the original study, before any re-analyst was anywhere near it.
:::
