:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
The aggregate answers the **contextual** question directly: does a country's framing move when its unemployment moves? What it cannot answer is the **compositional** one – whether it is the same people framing differently, or a different mix of people. There is a companion module that takes that up on simulated individual data.
:::

::: notes
Now, a practical matter with a conceptual sting in it. OA's data is Eurobarometer microdata under GESIS licence, which I am not permitted to redistribute – and, as you will see in a moment, that constraint is exactly what wrecked the first reproduction attempt on this paper. So what you get today is an aggregate I built from it and am allowed to share: two hundred and seventy country-years, one row each, with the framing scales averaged within each cell. It ships with both routes and it fits in milliseconds. The conceptual sting is on the fragment. The aggregate answers the contextual question directly – does a country's framing move when its unemployment moves. What it cannot answer is the compositional one: whether the same people are framing differently, or the mix of people has changed. If that interests you, there is a companion module on the site that takes it up on simulated individual data.
:::
## Reproducibility: two attempts, two failures

::: {.small}
- Data: openly available but not freely redistributable

::: {.claimcard .fragment}
"The required data to replicate my analyses can be downloaded on  the Gesis repository website. I am not allowed to forward the Eurobarometer data. Enclosed you´ll find the code to combine the different Eurobarometer data waves and the code for the analysis of the ESR piece"
:::

- Code: push-button reproduction failed

::: {.claimcard .fragment}
"The reproduction attempt failed because the authors used file names that did not correspond with the names of the files available for download. Additionally 16 datasets are listed on the website as being used but the code references 18 files"
:::

- **Source-data reproduction** (rebuild from raw) – **"not reproduced"**: could neither extract nor re-calculate the original effect size
:::

::: notes
So what happened when SCORE tried to reproduce this paper? Two attempts, two different failures. And let me be fair to OA here: there was no public archive with the paper, but OA did supply their two Stata do-files when asked – what OA could not share was the data, because GESIS terms do not allow it. Even with OA's code in hand, the push-button reproduction failed, and the report's wording is instructive – the file names in the code did not correspond to the files you could actually download; sixteen datasets listed, eighteen referenced. The second attempt rebuilt the data from source, and could not recover the published effect size at all. So this claim entered the robustness study already carrying two failed reproductions, of two different kinds.
:::

## Replication: the coefficient flips sign

::: {.small}
- Analysis One – the focal test on which SCORE evaluates the claim

  - 352,114 person-year observations in the analytic sample
  - b = 0.002, p = 0.046, se = 0.0008, t = 2.004

- Analysis Two – the "still studying" and "no full-time education" categories in the variable "age when finished full-timeeducation" were **not** converted to missing values

  - 379,396 person-year observations in the analytic sample
  - b = 0.002, p = 0.017, se = 0.0007, t = 2.394

- Both give a **positive coefficient** for unemployment on cosmopolitan framing, **significant** at p-values of 0.05 or less, after controlling for selected predictors and for wave and country-level effects
- By SCORE's criteria, Analysis Two did not replicate the claim
:::

::: {.src}
[osf.io/zt5y2/files/7efsw](https://osf.io/zt5y2/files/7efsw)
:::

## One paper, all three Rs

```{r}
#| label: score-scoreboard
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
# The full SCORE dossier on the EU-frames case as a clean three-row scoreboard
# (sources: osf.io/h7432 components; see resources page). Inline values, one
# row per R, colour-coded by verdict. Stays fully editable.
sb <- tibble::tribble(
  ~ord, ~R,              ~verdict,         ~detail,                                              ~fill,
  3,    "Reproducible?", "FAILED ×2", "push-button + source-data",  d_red,
  2,    "Robust?",       "MIXED",          "5 analysts, \nnegative effect in line with original, \nvaried strength + significance ", orange,
  1,    "Replicable?",   "FAILED",   "new Eurobarometer data, \nsign flipped/opposing results", d_red
)

ggplot(sb, aes(x = 1, y = ord)) +
  # role band
  geom_tile(aes(fill = fill), width = 0.9, height = 0.92,
            alpha = 0.14) +
  # left rule in the verdict colour
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0.553, xend = 0.553, y = ord - 0.46, yend = ord + 0.46,
                   colour = fill), linewidth = 6) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  # the R name
  geom_text(aes(label = R), x = 0.60, hjust = 0, vjust = 0.5,
            fontface = "bold", colour = ncl_blue, size = 8) +
  # the verdict
  geom_text(aes(label = verdict, colour = fill), x = 0.60, y = sb$ord - 0.26,
            hjust = 0, vjust = 0.5, fontface = "bold", size = 6.2) +
  # the supporting detail
  geom_text(aes(label = detail), x = 1.02, hjust = 0, vjust = 0.5,
            colour = grey_mid, size = 4.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.5, 1.9)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.4, 3.6)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_void()
```

::: {.src}
[osf.io/h7432](https://osf.io/h7432)
:::

::: notes
Put the whole dossier together – every artefact here is public, the link is on the slide. Reproduction: failed, twice, in two different ways. Robustness: mixed – five analysts, one sign, sizes spanning two orders of magnitude. And replication: a preregistered study took the same question to new Eurobarometer data, three hundred and fifty-two thousand observations – and the coefficient flipped sign. Positive, just significant, the wrong way round. So: one paper, three Rs, three different verdicts. That is the uncorrelated-indicators result from part one, embodied in a single case. Asking "is this paper reliable?" gets you nowhere; asking "reliable in which sense?" gets you all of this. Now – of the three, the middle one is where five careful people disagreed with each other, and it is the only one of the three we can do anything about today. So the rest of this part is about what they were disagreeing over.
:::

## Same verdict, five different questions {.smaller}

::: {.small}
| Analyst | Free-phase predictor | Free-phase outcome | Estimator |
|---|---|---|---|
| 018OL | GDP per capita (level) | positive framing, 7-item mean | crossed random intercepts |
| KEVF1 | GDP growth | positive framing, 7-item sum | random intercepts |
| PRL47 | log GDP + growth + crisis dummy | three positive-framing shares | three-level mixed |
| KQXUE | GDP growth **and** unemployment | cosmopolitan + utilitarian shares | country FE |
| **C6HJR** | **GDP growth and unemployment** | **positive framing, 7-item share** | **two-way FE** |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
- Five free analyses, **five different questions** – three of us never touched unemployment at all – and **one shared recorded verdict**: 'evidence for the claim'
- The constrained phase then *manufactured* a common question; its five comparable answers span **−0.006 to −0.45**
- Conclusions can agree while estimates cannot even be compared – the two robustness questions Multi100 was built to separate [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]
:::

::: {.src}
Free-phase records: the public Multi100 dataset (osf.io/q5h2c) – categorical verdicts and free-text reports only; the models themselves read from the analysts' public code.
:::

::: notes
Here is the layer underneath, and it is the sharpest illustration I have of this morning's point. Multi100 ran in two phases, and this table is the first one – months before the constrained task, complete freedom. Look at what freedom produced. GDP per capita for one analyst, GDP growth for another, a whole battery of GDP measures at three levels for a third – and three of the five of us never touched the unemployment rate at all. Different outcomes too: a mean, a sum, a share, three separate shares. Five different questions, in other words. And every single one of us recorded the same verdict: evidence for the claim. Then the constrained task arrived, manufactured one common question, and the five comparable answers ran from minus point zero zero six to minus point four five. Conclusions agreed in words while the numbers disagreed by two orders of magnitude. Now, that is five people on one paper. What happens when it is twenty-nine teams?
:::

## Two studies to set beside our five {.smaller}

::: {.small}
Our own case has just shown us the pattern in miniature. It was described first, and at far greater scale, somewhere else – and the two studies that did it are the ones the rest of this part rests on.
:::

:::: {.fragment}
::: {.small}
**Silberzahn and colleagues (2018)** – the red-card study from this morning. Twenty-nine teams, one dataset, one question. Twenty of the twenty-nine intervals excluded 1; nine did not.
:::

```{r}
#| label: silberzahn-strip
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 1.5

# as a reminder rather than a fresh argument. Hollow rings so the cluster

ggplot(silberzahn29, aes(or, y = 1, colour = significant)) +

                      breaks = c("TRUE", "FALSE"), name = NULL,
                      labels = c("significant", "not significant")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3)) +
```

::::

::: {.fragment .small}
**Auspurg and Brüderl (2021)** went back through all twenty-nine of those analyses and asked a question the original had not: what was each team actually trying to measure?
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The first establishes that careful people disagree. The second explains **why** – and that explanation is what the whole of Part 2 is built on.
:::

::: {.src}
@SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne; @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial
:::

::: notes
Before we go further into our own case, I want to put two studies beside it – and one of them you have already met. Silberzahn and colleagues, the red-card study from this morning: twenty-nine teams, one dataset, one question, twenty intervals excluding one and nine not. There are all twenty-nine again, flattened onto a single line so you can see the shape rather than read the table. That is the study that establishes careful people disagree. The second one is new, and it is the hinge of this part. Auspurg and Brüderl, twenty twenty-one, went back through all twenty-nine of those pipelines and asked something the original had not thought to ask: what was each team actually trying to measure? So one study shows the disagreement, and the other explains it. Let me take the second one properly.
:::

## They were not answering the same question

:::: {.none}
<br>
Auspurg & Brüderl re-read the 29 analyses and found **four** different estimands:

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
descriptive association · discrimination *net of mediators* · variance-maximising · exploratory
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
The dispersion was largely a **question**-multiverse, not an analysis-multiverse.
:::
::::

::: {.src}
@AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial
:::

::: notes
And here is what they found, which is the hinge of this morning: the teams were not answering one question. They found four. Some estimated the plain descriptive association. Some went after discrimination proper – the effect net of everything that legitimately explains red cards. Some built models tuned to explain variance. And some were frankly exploring. Of course the answers differed – they were answers to different questions. That reframes the crisis quite a bit: much of what looks like analytical instability is unstated disagreement about *what is being estimated*.
:::


## Fix the estimand, and the spread collapses

```{r}
#| label: redcard-contrast
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.2
# Dispersion contrast. TOP ROW IS REAL: the 29 published estimates, same file
# the Part 1 forest reads. BOTTOM ROW IS A SKETCH: Auspurg & Brüderl give the
# median (1.28) and SD (0.06) of their 486-model multiverse but not the 486
# values, so these are evenly spaced quantiles of a normal on exactly those two
# numbers - deterministic, and reproducing the published summary by
# construction rather than by a lucky seed.
ab <- qnorm(seq(0.5, 485.5, by = 1) / 486, mean = 1.28, sd = 0.06)
contrast <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(grp = "29 teams,\nquestion left open", or = silberzahn29$or),
  tibble::tibble(grp = "486 models,\nestimand fixed", or = ab)
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(grp = factor(grp, levels = c("486 models,\nestimand fixed",
                                             "29 teams,\nquestion left open")))

ggplot(contrast, aes(or, grp, colour = grp)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "longdash", colour = grey_mid) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, fill = NA, size = 4.6, stroke = 1.1, alpha = 0.75) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.0, y = 2.42, label = "SD 0.45", hjust = 1,
           colour = d_red, fontface = "bold", size = 4.6) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.0, y = 1.42, label = "SD 0.06", hjust = 1,
           colour = ncl_blue, fontface = "bold", size = 4.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(ncl_blue, d_red)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.8, 3.05), ylim = c(0.7, 2.6)) +
  labs(x = "odds ratio", y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(14) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = "grey92"))
```

::: {.small}
- Fix the question → derive the model space from a DAG → run **all 486** justifiable models → **SD 0.45 → 0.06**
- The top row's spread is **two analyses wide**: a tight cluster plus the two outliers, which are what carry that 0.45
:::

::: {.src}
@AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial. Top row: the 29 published estimates. Bottom row: drawn to their reported median (1.28) and SD (0.06) – the 486 values are not published.
:::

::: notes
And here is the optimistic half of the red-card story. Auspurg and Brüderl fixed one estimand – discrimination, properly defined – used a causal graph to derive every model specification consistent with it, four hundred and eighty-six of them, and ran the lot. Look what happens to the spread: standard deviation point four five in the crowd, point zero six with the question fixed. Same caveat as before – these strips are sketches from the published summary figures. The recipe we take from them is the workshop's recipe: a precise question, assumptions drawn out explicitly, then a whole multiverse rather than one path, then sensitivity analysis. And notice where the spread in the top row actually comes from – a tight cluster and two outliers, which is why the standard deviation is four times what the cluster alone would give you. Fix the question and even those go. [advance]
:::


## The crisis has a crisis of its own {.smaller}

:::: {.none}
Auspurg and Brüderl's title asks it directly: *has the credibility of the social sciences been credibly destroyed?*

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
If the twenty-nine teams answered **four different questions**, their disagreement is not evidence that analysis is unreliable.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
It is evidence that **the question was under-specified** – an ordinary, fixable defect.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
So this literature is not a verdict on social science. It is a **diagnosis of vague research questions**.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
More optimistic – and more demanding, because it hands the problem to whoever writes the question.
:::
::::

::: {.src}
@AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial
:::

::: notes
Now, this diagnosis has a consequence that goes well beyond the red-card study, and Auspurg and Brüderl put it in their title: has the credibility of the social sciences been credibly destroyed? Follow the logic. If the twenty-nine teams were in fact answering four different questions, then their disagreement is not evidence that data analysis is unreliable. It is evidence that the question they were handed was under-specified – and that is an ordinary, fixable defect of research design, not a crisis of method. Read that way, the whole many-analyst literature stops being a verdict on the field and becomes a diagnosis of vague research questions. I find that a considerably more optimistic reading. It is also a more demanding one, because it takes the problem away from statistics, where you could hope a better estimator would save you, and puts it back on the person writing the question. That person is you.
:::
## What is your estimand?

```{r}
#| label: lundberg-pipeline
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3
# Lundberg et al. (2021) three steps as boxes-and-arrows (ggplot, editable).
steps <- tibble::tibble(
  x = c(1, 2, 3),
  lab = c("Theoretical\nestimand",
          "Empirical\nestimand",
          "Estimation\nstrategy"),
  sub = c("unit quantity +\ntarget population",
          "identification\nassumptions (DAG)",
          "where the R\ncode enters")
)
ggplot(steps, aes(x, 1)) +
  geom_tile(width = 0.8, height = 0.7, fill = ncl_blue) +
  geom_text(aes(label = lab), colour = "white", fontface = "bold",
            size = 5.2, vjust = -0.3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sub), colour = "white", size = 3.6, vjust = 2.0) +
  annotate("segment", x = 1.42, xend = 1.58, y = 1, yend = 1,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm")), linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("segment", x = 2.42, xend = 2.58, y = 1, yend = 1,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm")), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.5, 3.5)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_void()
```

::: {.none}
- The theoretical estimand is stated **outside** any model – before R opens
:::

::: {.src}
@LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand.
:::

::: notes
Which brings us to the most useful question in quantitative research: what is your estimand? Lundberg and colleagues split the answer into three steps. First, the theoretical estimand: a unit-specific quantity and a target population, stated in plain words, before any model exists. Second, the empirical estimand: what in the observable data corresponds to that quantity – and making that link forces your identification assumptions into the open, which is exactly where the causal graph lives. Only third comes estimation, where R finally opens. When they audited a full year of papers in a top sociology journal, the unit quantity was clearly stated in five out of thirty-two. Their demand is the one to remember: every quantitative study must be able to answer the question – what is your estimand?
:::

## DAG crash course: three roles {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: mini-dags
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
# Three tiny DAGs: confounder / mediator / collider. Each arrow is an R formula
# read outcome-first, so `X ~ Z` is the arrow Z -> X; dagify() takes the
# coordinates, the exposure and the outcome in the same call, and returns a
# plain dagitty object that adjustmentSets() and paths() accept unchanged.
conf <- ggdag::dagify(X ~ Z, Y ~ X + Z,
  coords = list(x = c(X = 0, Y = 2, Z = 1), y = c(X = 0, Y = 0, Z = 1)))
med  <- ggdag::dagify(M ~ X, Y ~ M + X,
  coords = list(x = c(X = 0, Y = 2, M = 1), y = c(X = 0, Y = 0, M = 1)))
coll <- ggdag::dagify(C ~ X + Y, Y ~ X,
  coords = list(x = c(X = 0, Y = 2, C = 1), y = c(X = 0, Y = 0, C = -1)))

# Edges are coloured by role: the X -> Y causal effect (the estimand) is GREEN
# in every panel; the secondary structure carries an accent – RED where it
# biases the naive estimate (the confounder fork, the collider edges) and AMBER
# for the mediator's indirect path, which is part of the total effect rather
# than bias. The accent is passed per panel; green is constant so the eye learns
# 'green = the effect I want, coloured = the path I must reason about'.
gg <- function(d, ttl, cap, accent = d_red) {
  td <- ggdag::tidy_dagitty(d)
  td$data <- dplyr::mutate(td$data,
    edge_kind = dplyr::if_else(name == "X" & to == "Y", "causal", "other"))
  ggplot2::ggplot(td,
      ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
    ggdag::geom_dag_edges(ggplot2::aes(edge_colour = edge_kind),
      arrow_directed = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(7, "pt"),
                                   type = "closed")) +
    ggdag::geom_dag_point(size = 16, colour = "black") +
    ggdag::geom_dag_text(colour = "white", size = 4) +
    ggraph::scale_edge_colour_manual(
      values = c(causal = green, other = accent), guide = "none") +
    ggdag::theme_dag() +
    # Expand the panel so the nodes sit well inside it – otherwise the title
    # and caption crowd (and slightly cover) the top/bottom nodes.
    ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.18)) +
    ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.32)) +
    ggplot2::labs(title = ttl, caption = cap) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ncl_blue,
                                hjust = 0.5, size = 16,
                                margin = margin(b = 10)),
      plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 11,
                                  colour = grey_mid, lineheight = 1.05,
                                  margin = margin(t = 10)))
}
  patchwork::wrap_plots(
    gg(conf, "Confounder Z",
       "Common cause of X and Y.\nADJUST – or the estimate is biased.", d_red),
    gg(med,  "Mediator M",
       "Sits on the path X → Y.\nDON'T adjust for the total effect.", orange),
    gg(coll, "Collider C",
       "Caused by both X and Y.\nNEVER adjust – it opens a spurious path.", d_red),
    nrow = 1)
```

::: {.src}
X = predictor, Y = outcome. **Green** = the causal effect you want; **coloured** = the path you must reason about.
:::

::: notes
All the graph theory you need today, in three small pictures. In every panel the green arrow is the same thing – the effect you are actually after, X on Y. What changes is the coloured structure around it. A confounder is a common cause of your predictor and your outcome – that red fork is a back-door path, and if you leave it open you are biased, so you adjust to close it. A mediator sits on the causal path between them – the amber path is real, it is part of the total effect, so if the total effect is what you want you do not adjust for it, or you remove part of the very thing you are measuring. And a collider is caused by both sides – those edges are harmless until you condition on the collider, which opens a spurious path that was not there before. So the rulebook is short: adjust confounders, leave mediators alone for total effects, and never condition on a collider. That is the entire toolkit – the next four slides just give it a bit more depth before you use it.
:::

## One number, many stories {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}

```{r}
#| label: many-stories
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 4.3
# A single strong association. The same slope is consistent with several
# different causal structures – the number alone cannot tell you which one
# generated it (the 'causal quartet' point). Scatter is simulated for display.
set.seed(11)
n <- 130; x <- rnorm(n); y <- 0.6 * x + rnorm(n, 0, 0.85)
df <- tibble::tibble(x, y)
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(colour = ncl_blue, alpha = 0.5, size = 2.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = d_red, linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("text", x = min(x), y = max(y), hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
           label = paste0("r = ", format(round(cor(x, y), 2), nsmall = 2)),
           colour = d_red, fontface = "bold", size = 6.5) +
  labs(x = "X", y = "Y") + theme_slide(16)
```

:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.small}
The same slope fits four different stories:

::: {.fragment}
- X really causes Y – the slope *is* the effect
:::
::: {.fragment}
- a common cause inflates it – **confounding**
:::
::: {.fragment}
- we are seeing a selected sample – **collider / selection**
:::
::: {.fragment}
- Y causes X (**reverse causation**), or it is **chance**
:::
::: {.fragment}
The data look identical in all four. Only an assumption about *how the data arose* tells them apart – that is what a DAG writes down.
:::
:::
:::
::::

::: {.src}
@DAgostinoMcGowanEtAl2024CausalInferenceNot; @KeeleEtAl2020CausalInterpretationEstimated. Scatter simulated for illustration.
:::

::: notes
Here is a strong correlation – r of about nought point six. Before you reach for a model, sit with an uncomfortable fact: this single number is consistent with at least four different stories. Maybe X really does cause Y, and the slope is the effect. Maybe a common cause is inflating it. Maybe we are quietly looking at a selected sample, and the association is an artefact of who got in. Maybe Y causes X, or it is simply chance. The data cannot choose between these – the scatter looks identical in every case. Only a claim about how the data were generated can. That claim is what a DAG writes down, and it is why we draw one before we fit anything.
:::

## Reading a DAG: open and closed paths {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: backdoor-paths
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 3.7
# Same confounder graph, twice. LEFT: the back-door path X <- Z -> Y is open
# (red), so the naive X -> Y estimate is biased. RIGHT: adjusting for Z (boxed)
# blocks the back-door (greyed), leaving the green causal path clean. Reuses
# `conf` from the mini-dags chunk.
path_panel <- function(adjust_z = FALSE) {
  td <- ggdag::tidy_dagitty(conf)
  td$data <- dplyr::mutate(td$data,
    edge_kind = dplyr::if_else(name == "X" & to == "Y", "causal",
                       if (adjust_z) "blocked" else "backdoor"))
  p <- ggplot2::ggplot(td,
      ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
    ggdag::geom_dag_edges(ggplot2::aes(edge_colour = edge_kind),
      arrow_directed = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(7, "pt"),
                                   type = "closed")) +
    ggdag::geom_dag_point(size = 18, colour = "black") +
    ggdag::geom_dag_text(colour = "white", size = 4.4) +
    ggraph::scale_edge_colour_manual(
      values = c(causal = green, backdoor = d_red, blocked = grey_mid),
      guide = "none") +
    ggdag::theme_dag() +
    ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.22)) +
    ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.40)) +
    ggplot2::labs(title = if (adjust_z) "Adjust for Z → back-door closed"
                          else "Back-door path X ← Z → Y is open") +
    ggplot2::theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ncl_blue,
                                hjust = 0.5, size = 15, margin = margin(b = 8)))
  if (adjust_z) {
    zc <- subset(td$data, name == "Z")[1, ]
    p <- p + ggplot2::annotate("point", x = zc$x, y = zc$y, shape = 0,
                               size = 14, stroke = 1.6, colour = ncl_blue)
  }
  p
}
patchwork::wrap_plots(path_panel(FALSE), path_panel(TRUE), nrow = 1)
```

::: {.small}
Association flows along **every open path**, not only along the causal arrow. A fork or a chain is open until you adjust the variable sitting on it. A collider is the reverse: shut by default, and opened by the very act of adjusting for it.

- **Back-door criterion**: close every path that enters X from behind, keep the causal X → Y path open
- That adjustment set – and only that set – earns a causal reading
:::

::: {.src}
@HernanRobins2020CausalInferenceWhat; @Huntington-Klein2021EffectIntroductionResearch.
:::

::: notes
A DAG is read through its paths. Association does not only travel down the causal arrow – it flows along every open path between X and Y. So the job is to work out which paths are open and shut the ones you do not want. Two rules do all the work. A path through a fork or a chain is open, and you close it by adjusting the variable in the middle – that is the red back-door fork on the left. A path through a collider is the opposite: shut by default, and you open it by adjusting. The back-door criterion just packages this: close every path that sneaks into X from behind, leave the causal X-to-Y path alone. The set that does that – and only that set – is what you are allowed to read as causal.
:::

## Which effect do you even want? {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| label: total-direct
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.1
# Mediator graph with the two routes coloured: the DIRECT effect X -> Y (green)
# and the INDIRECT route X -> M -> Y (amber). Together they make the total
# effect; adjusting for M leaves only the direct one. Reuses `med`.
td <- ggdag::tidy_dagitty(med)
td$data <- dplyr::mutate(td$data,
  edge_kind = dplyr::if_else(name == "X" & to == "Y", "direct", "indirect"))
ggplot2::ggplot(td,
    ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
  ggdag::geom_dag_edges(ggplot2::aes(edge_colour = edge_kind),
    arrow_directed = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(8, "pt"), type = "closed")) +
  ggdag::geom_dag_point(size = 22, colour = "black") +
  ggdag::geom_dag_text(colour = "white", size = 5) +
  ggraph::scale_edge_colour_manual(values = c(direct = green, indirect = orange),
    guide = "none") +
  ggdag::theme_dag() +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.18)) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.30)) +
  ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.62, label = "indirect", colour = orange,
           fontface = "bold", size = 4.5, angle = 33) +
  ggplot2::annotate("text", x = 1, y = -0.14, label = "direct", colour = green,
           fontface = "bold", size = 4.5)
```

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.small}
- **Total** = direct (green) + indirect (amber)
- Adjust for the mediator M → you estimate the **direct** effect only – a *different* estimand
- 'Control for everything' silently answers a question you never asked
- **Table 2 fallacy**: the other coefficients in your model are *not* all causal effects
:::
:::
::::

::: {.src}
@KeeleEtAl2020CausalInterpretationEstimated; @DAgostinoMcGowanEtAl2024CausalInferenceNot.
:::

::: notes
Now the question the estimand discussion was circling. Suppose M sits between your predictor and outcome. The total effect is the green arrow plus the amber route through M. The direct effect is just the green arrow. These are different numbers and different questions – and which one you get depends entirely on whether you put M in the model. Drop a mediator in as just another 'control' and you have silently switched to the direct effect without telling anyone, including yourself. This is why 'control for everything' is bad advice. And it has a famous corollary – the Table 2 fallacy: when you print a regression table, usually only one coefficient has a clean causal reading. The control variables' coefficients are not little causal effects of their own.
:::

## Spurious by design: selection & feedback {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: selection-panel
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.7
# LEFT: a collider S caused by A and B. Conditioning on (or sampling on) S –
# the red box – induces a spurious A–B association (dashed red). RIGHT: a
# two-wave cross-lagged panel. The claim U1 -> F2 is green; the reverse path
# F1 -> U2 is red; the autoregressive paths are grey. Two-way FE handles
# neither feedback nor time-varying confounding.
sel <- ggdag::dagify(S ~ A + B,
  coords = list(x = c(A = 0, S = 1, B = 2), y = c(A = 0, S = 1, B = 0)))
tds <- ggdag::tidy_dagitty(sel)
tds$data <- dplyr::mutate(tds$data, edge_kind = "structural")
p_sel <- ggplot2::ggplot(tds,
    ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
  ggdag::geom_dag_edges(ggplot2::aes(edge_colour = edge_kind),
    arrow_directed = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(7, "pt"), type = "closed")) +
  ggdag::geom_dag_point(size = 18, colour = "black") +
  ggdag::geom_dag_text(colour = "white", size = 4.4) +
  ggraph::scale_edge_colour_manual(values = c(structural = grey_mid), guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::annotate("point", x = 1, y = 1, shape = 0, size = 14, stroke = 1.6,
                    colour = d_red) +
  ggplot2::annotate("curve", x = 0.12, y = -0.18, xend = 1.88, yend = -0.18,
    curvature = -0.25, colour = d_red, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9,
    arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(6, "pt"), ends = "both")) +
  ggdag::theme_dag() +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.22)) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.45)) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Condition on collider S → spurious A–B link") +
  ggplot2::theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ncl_blue,
                              hjust = 0.5, size = 14, margin = margin(b = 8)))

clp <- ggdag::dagify(U2 ~ U1 + F1, F2 ~ F1 + U1,
  coords = list(x = c(U1 = 0, F1 = 0, U2 = 2, F2 = 2),
                y = c(U1 = 1, F1 = 0, U2 = 1, F2 = 0)))
tdc <- ggdag::tidy_dagitty(clp)
tdc$data <- dplyr::mutate(tdc$data, edge_kind = dplyr::case_when(
  name == "U1" & to == "F2" ~ "claim",
  name == "F1" & to == "U2" ~ "reverse",
  TRUE ~ "auto"))
p_clp <- ggplot2::ggplot(tdc,
    ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
  ggdag::geom_dag_edges(ggplot2::aes(edge_colour = edge_kind),
    arrow_directed = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(7, "pt"), type = "closed")) +
  ggdag::geom_dag_point(size = 20, colour = "black") +
  ggdag::geom_dag_text(colour = "white", size = 3.6) +
  ggraph::scale_edge_colour_manual(
    values = c(claim = green, reverse = d_red, auto = grey_mid), guide = "none") +
  ggdag::theme_dag() +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.18)) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = 0.30)) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Panel feedback: U now → F later, but also F → U") +
  ggplot2::theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ncl_blue,
                              hjust = 0.5, size = 14, margin = margin(b = 8)))
patchwork::wrap_plots(p_sel, p_clp, nrow = 1)
```

::: {.small}
- **Selection / collider bias** – conditioning, or merely *sampling*, on a common effect manufactures an association that was never there (much of the early COVID risk-factor literature)
- **Reverse causation & feedback** – in a panel, today's outcome can move tomorrow's predictor; two-way fixed effects absorb stable country traits and common-year shocks, **not** time-varying feedback (U = unemployment, F = framing)
:::

::: {.src}
@GriffithEtAl2020ColliderBiasUndermines; @ColeEtAl2010IllustratingBiasDue; @LeszczenskyWolbring2022HowDealReverse.
:::

::: notes
Two last ways a relationship can be spurious, both of which live in our case. The first is selection, or collider bias. If you condition on – or merely sample on – something that both your variables cause, you manufacture a correlation out of nothing. A lot of the early COVID risk-factor findings were exactly this: conclusions drawn from people who had been tested, which is a selected group. The second is reverse causation and feedback. Our data are a panel, and in a panel today's outcome can feed tomorrow's predictor. Two-way fixed effects – which is the model we are about to draw – soak up stable differences between countries and shocks common to a year. They do not, on their own, fix a time-varying confounder or a feedback loop. Keep that in mind when we build the graph for our own paper.
:::

## *Revenons à nos moutons*

::: {.claimcard}
"The expected change in [unit quantity] among [target population] for a 1-percentage-point difference in unemployment, holding [assumptions] fixed."
:::

::: {.small}
- Unit quantity – a *person's* cosmopolitan framing, or a *country-year* mean?
- Target population – which countries, which years?
:::

::: {.fragment}
**In chat, now:** your one-sentence estimand for the claim. Type it, hold it, send on "go".
:::

::: notes
Now apply it to our paper – and this one is a chat exercise. Write the sentence on the slide with the brackets filled in: your one-sentence estimand for the claim. Type it, hold it, send when I say go. [go; read three or four aloud.] Look at the spread in the chat – some of you wrote about a person's framing, some about a country-year average, some named different years. None of those are wrong; they are different questions, with different confounding stories, and the coefficient means something different in each. That spread, in a room that just watched the same slides, is the red-card diagnosis happening live. Keep your sentence – it goes into your preregistration this afternoon, and this afternoon you will also see what the unit choice did to the five published analysts.
:::

## We cannot identify a causal effect here {.smaller}

::: {.small}
Observational panel · 27 countries · no assignment mechanism · feedback between the variables · a decade of shared shocks.

Nothing in this design licenses "unemployment **causes** a shift in EU framing".
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
So why spend half an hour on causal graphs?
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Because the graph does three jobs that survive the loss of identification:

- It says **which association** you are after – the total effect, not whatever the software returns
- It tells you **which variables belong in the model**, and, just as usefully, which do not
- It makes your assumptions **legible and arguable** – a reader can disagree with an arrow, and that is a productive disagreement
:::

::: notes
Let me be blunt about where we stand. This is an observational panel of twenty-seven countries. Nobody assigned unemployment to anyone. The variables plausibly feed back into each other over time, and the whole decade is shot through with shocks that hit everybody at once. Nothing in that design licenses the sentence "unemployment causes a shift in EU framing". So why are we about to spend half an hour on causal graphs? Because the graph does three jobs that survive perfectly well without identification. It says which association you are actually after – the total effect, say, rather than whatever the software happens to return. It tells you which variables belong in your model, and just as usefully which do not. And it puts your assumptions on paper where a reader can disagree with a specific arrow. That last one is the real prize: an argument about an arrow is a productive argument, and an argument about a coefficient usually is not.
:::

## Say it in public, or it does not count {.smaller}

::: {.small}
The graph and the estimand are only worth anything if they are **written down where someone else can read them**:

- in the paper, not in your head
- **before** the model runs, not reconstructed afterwards
- with the **limitations named by you**, not discovered by a reviewer
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
This is the thread that ties the day together. In Part 4 you write exactly that down – the estimand, the graph-based justification, the one specification, and the rule for what would count as support – and you do it **before** you see a result.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The technical name for that is preregistration. What it really is: refusing to let the result choose the question.
:::

::: notes
And one more step, which is where the day is heading. A graph you drew and did not publish is worth almost nothing. It has to be written down where someone else can read it – in the paper, not in your head. It has to be written before the model runs, not reconstructed afterwards once you know which way the coefficient went, because a graph drawn after the fact will very reliably justify the result you already have. And the limitations have to be named by you, not discovered by a reviewer. That is the thread running through the rest of today. In part four you will write exactly that down: your estimand, your graph-based justification, the one specification you commit to, and your rule for what would count as support – and you will do it before you see a result. The technical name for it is preregistration. What it actually is, is refusing to let the result choose the question.
:::
## The EU-frames DAG, half built

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}

```{r}
#| label: teney-dag
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 5.8
# ggdag rendering of the Task-C starter DAG. This reproduces the EXACT graph in
# _template/R/dag_starter.R: the causal path of interest and the two confounder
# pairs (country, year) are drawn SOLID; the three arguable nodes (growth,
# bailout, politicisation) are present but UNCONNECTED – the edges participants
# decide whether to add in Task 4. That is what makes it 'half built'. Nodes are
# coloured by ROLE (predictor orange, outcome navy, candidates light grey),
# labels sit inside the nodes in white/dark, edges are thick and gently curved.
dag <- ggdag::dagify(
  framing ~ unemployment,
  framing ~ country + year,
  unemployment ~ country + year,
  exposure = "unemployment",
  outcome  = "framing",
  coords = list(
    x = c(unemployment = 0, framing = 3, country = 1, year = 2),
    y = c(unemployment = 0, framing = 0, country = 1.4, year = 1.4)))

# dagify() has no way to hold a node with no edges, so the three candidates
# join the picture at the tidy-data layer instead. 'growth' is nudged down off
# the year -> unemployment crossing arrow; the other two are kept clear of the
# committed edges.
candidates <- tibble::tribble(
  ~name,             ~x,    ~y,
  "growth",           0.9, -1.0,
  "bailout",          1.5, -1.2,
  "politicisation",   3.0, -0.95)

# Role lookup → drives node fill and label colour; short display labels keep
# the longer names from overflowing the nodes (the underlying graph keeps the
# full names, matching dag_starter.R).
roles <- tibble::tibble(
  name = c("unemployment", "framing", "country", "year",
           "growth", "bailout", "politicisation"),
  role = c("predictor", "outcome", "adjusted", "adjusted",
           "candidate", "candidate", "candidate"),
  disp = c("unemp.", "framing", "country", "year",
           "growth", "bailout", "politic."))
role_fill <- c(predictor = orange, outcome = ncl_blue,
               adjusted = "#c7ccd2", candidate = "#dde2e7")
# White labels read on the dark predictor/outcome fills; navy on the light greys.
role_lab  <- c(predictor = "#FFFFFF", outcome = "#FFFFFF",
               adjusted = ncl_blue, candidate = "#5d666e")

dag_tidy <- ggdag::tidy_dagitty(dag)
ggdag::update_dag_data(dag_tidy) <- ggdag::pull_dag_data(dag_tidy) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows(candidates) |>
  dplyr::left_join(roles, by = "name") |>
  dplyr::mutate(role = factor(role,
    levels = c("predictor", "outcome", "adjusted", "candidate")))

ggplot2::ggplot(dag_tidy,
    ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
  # geom_dag_edges_arc() takes `arrow`, not the `arrow_directed` of
  # geom_dag_edges(); and the nodes are wide enough to paint over an arrowhead,
  # so end_cap stops each edge short of the circle it points at.
  ggdag::geom_dag_edges_arc(curvature = 0.18, edge_colour = grey_mid,
                            edge_width = 1.1,
                            end_cap = ggraph::circle(11, "mm"),
                            arrow = grid::arrow(
                              length = grid::unit(9, "pt"), type = "closed")) +
  ggdag::geom_dag_point(ggplot2::aes(fill = role), shape = 21,
                        size = 32, stroke = 0, colour = "white") +
  ggdag::geom_dag_text(ggplot2::aes(label = disp, colour = role),
                       size = 5.2, fontface = "bold") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = role_fill, guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = role_lab, guide = "none") +
  ggdag::theme_dag() +
  ggplot2::expand_limits(x = c(-0.7, 3.7), y = c(-1.9, 2.1)) +
  ggplot2::theme(plot.margin = ggplot2::margin(14, 14, 14, 14))
```

::: {.dagcode}
The same graph in R. Every arrow is a formula, read outcome-first – so a `#` takes an arrow out and the code still runs:
:::

```r
dagify(
  framing ~ unemployment,
  framing ~ country + year,
  unemployment ~ country + year,
  # framing ~ growth,        # uncomment the
  # unemployment ~ growth,   # arrows you believe
  exposure = "unemployment", outcome = "framing"
) |> adjustmentSets()
```
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.small}
- Drawn: the path + two confounder pairs (**country, year → two-way FE**)
- Floating, unwired: growth (confounder?) · bailout (mediator?) · politicisation (mediator?)
- You add the edges you believe, then run `adjustmentSets()`
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
And here is the graph you will finish yourselves. The solid part is what we are committing to: unemployment to framing is the path of interest, and country and year are the two confounder pairs – stable national traits on one side, EU-wide shocks in a given year on the other. Run `adjustmentSets()` on this graph and it answers: country and year. Which is precisely what a two-way fixed-effects model absorbs – the graph and the baseline model are the same claim, written in two languages. The three pale nodes are yours to wire up, and they are genuine decisions. Is GDP growth a time-varying confounder that fixed effects cannot reach – a slump that raises unemployment and sours sentiment in the same year? Is the bailout a mediator, in which case you leave it alone if you want the total effect? Multi100 told us to disregard politicisation – was that defensible? The code beside the picture is the same graph written as R formulas, one arrow to a line, so wiring a node up is uncommenting the line you believe and running it again to see what the adjustment set has become. Whatever you decide here becomes your model in the next task – that is the point.
:::

     out the region between this marker and DEEP DIVE END. Every slide in the
     run also carries the .deepdive class. -->

## R, in one slide {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.skiplink}
[10 optional slides · skip to Hands-on 2 →](#hands-on-2-meet-the-panel-draw-the-graph)
:::

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|3|5|7"}
x <- 42                          # <- assigns. "x gets 42"

mean(c(2, 4, 6))                 # a function: name, then arguments in ()

euframes$unemp                   # $ picks one column out of a data frame

euframes |> nrow()               # |> the pipe: send the left into the right
```

::: {.small}
Four things and you can read most R: **assign** with `<-` · **call** a function with `name(...)` · **reach into** an object with `$` · **chain** with the pipe `|>`.
:::

::: notes
If you have never written a line of R, this slide is most of what you need to read the rest. Four things. First, the arrow assigns: x gets forty-two. You will see the equals sign used the same way and both work, but the arrow is the convention and it reads better out loud. Second, a function is a name followed by round brackets containing its arguments – mean of two, four and six. Third, the dollar sign reaches inside an object to pull out one column. And fourth, the pipe, which is the one that changes how the code reads: it takes whatever is on its left and feeds it in as the first argument of whatever is on its right. So euframes pipe nrow means "take euframes, and count its rows". Once you see the pipe as the word "then", long chains become readable sentences.
:::

## Getting data in {.smaller .deepdive}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|3|5"}
library(readr)                                # load a package

euframes <- read_csv("data/EUframes_cy.csv")  # read it, name it

euframes                                      # print it
```

::: {.small}
What comes back is a **data frame**: a rectangle, one row per observation, one column per variable, each column of a single type. Almost everything in R takes a data frame and gives you one back.

`library()` makes a package's functions available. It does **not** install it – that is `install.packages()`, and it happens once, not every time.
:::

::: notes
Getting data in. The library line makes a package's functions available for this session – and note that it does not install anything; installing is a separate thing you do once. Then read underscore csv reads the file and the arrow gives the result a name, so from here on euframes is our panel. Typing the name on its own prints it. What you get back is a data frame, which is R's central object: a rectangle with one row per observation, one column per variable, and each column holding a single type. Nearly every function you will meet takes a data frame and hands you a data frame back, which is why the pipe works so well – the output of one step is the right shape to be the input of the next.
:::

## Look before you model {.smaller .deepdive}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|2|3|5-6"}
glimpse(euframes)      # every column, its type, the first few values
nrow(euframes)         # 270
summary(euframes$unemp)  # min, quartiles, mean, max

euframes |>
  count(cntry)         # how many rows per country?
```

::: {.fragment .small}
This is not a warm-up you skip. Every serious error I have made in twenty years of this was visible in the data before it reached a model – a duplicated year, a missing value coded as `-9`, a scale running 1–10 where I assumed 0–1.
:::

::: notes
Look before you model. Glimpse shows every column with its type and first few values. nrow counts the rows. Summary on a single column gives the minimum, the quartiles, the mean and the maximum. And count, piped, tells you how many rows there are per country – which for a balanced panel should be the same number every time. Now, the fragment there is not a rhetorical flourish. Every serious error I have made in twenty years of doing this was visible in the data before it ever reached a model: a year that appeared twice, a missing value coded as minus nine and quietly averaged in, a scale running one to ten when I had assumed nought to one. Ten minutes of looking is the highest-return ten minutes in the whole workflow, and it is the part people skip because it does not feel like analysis.
:::

## Five verbs do most of the work {.smaller .deepdive}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|2|3|4|5"}
euframes |>
  filter(year >= 2008) |>                       # keep some rows
  select(cntry, year, mcosmo, unemp) |>         # keep some columns
  mutate(unemp_c = unemp - mean(unemp)) |>      # make a new column
  arrange(desc(unemp))                          # sort
```

::: {.small}
Read it downwards as a sentence: *take the panel, then keep 2008 onwards, then keep four columns, then add a centred unemployment column, then sort by unemployment, highest first.*
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The sixth verb is `summarise()`, usually with `group_by()`: collapse many rows into one per group. That is precisely how the panel you are working on was built from 390,000 respondents.
:::

::: notes
Five verbs get you a very long way, and they all work the same way: first argument a data frame, result a data frame. Filter keeps rows. Select keeps columns. Mutate makes a new column. Arrange sorts. And the pipe strings them together so you read the whole thing downwards as a sentence: take the panel, then keep 2008 onwards, then keep these four columns, then add a centred unemployment column, then sort by unemployment with the highest first. The sixth verb, on the fragment, is summarise, usually paired with group-by: collapse many rows into one row per group. That is worth naming because it is exactly the operation that produced the panel you will be working on – three hundred and ninety thousand respondents collapsed into two hundred and seventy country-year means.
:::

## A model is a formula plus data {.smaller .deepdive}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|3|5"}
mcosmo ~ unemp                    # "mcosmo explained by unemp"

m <- lm(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = euframes)

summary(m)
```

::: {.small}
The tilde `~` reads **outcome on the left, predictors on the right**. Add predictors with `+`. The formula is an object in its own right – it does not know or care which function will eventually use it.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Almost every modelling function in R takes this same shape: `something(formula, data = ...)`. Learn the pattern once and `lm`, `glm`, `lmer`, `feols` and `betareg` all become variations.
:::

::: notes
Now models. The tilde is the heart of it: outcome on the left, predictors on the right, and you add more predictors with a plus. The thing that surprises people coming from other software is that the formula is an object in its own right – you can store it in a variable, print it, pass it around – and it has no idea which function will eventually use it. Then lm fits a linear model given that formula and a data frame, the arrow names the result, and summary prints the coefficient table. The genuinely useful pattern is on the fragment: almost every modelling function in R has this same shape, something bracket formula comma data. Learn it once and lm, glm, lmer for multilevel models, feols for fixed effects and betareg for bounded outcomes all become variations on one thing you already know.
:::

## Fixed effects, the fast way {.smaller .deepdive}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|3|3"}
library(fixest)

m1 <- feols(mcosmo ~ unemp_c | cntry + year, data = euframes)
```

::: {.small}
The bar `|` separates the regression from the **fixed effects**. Everything after it is absorbed: `cntry` gives every country its own intercept, `year` gives every year its own.

The equivalent with dummies would be `mcosmo ~ unemp_c + factor(cntry) + factor(year)` – same estimate, 36 extra rows of output you do not want to read.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
This is the model you reproduce in Part 3. **`t = −3.804`.**
:::

::: notes
This one you will type yourself in a couple of hours, so it is worth a slow look. Feols comes from the fixest package and fits linear models with fixed effects very fast. The bar is the key piece of syntax: everything to the left of it is the regression, everything to the right is absorbed as fixed effects. Country gives every country its own intercept, so we are comparing each country with itself over time rather than comparing countries with each other. Year gives every year its own intercept, so anything that hit all of Europe in a given year is soaked up. You could write the same model with dummy variables – the estimate would be identical – but you would get thirty-six extra rows of output that nobody wants to read. And this exact line is the model you reproduce in part three, landing on minus three point eight zero four.
:::

## Reading what comes back {.smaller .deepdive}

```{.r}
broom::tidy(m1)
#> term      estimate    std.error   statistic   p.value
#> unemp_c   -0.00347    0.00091     -3.80       0.00019
```

::: {.small}
- **estimate** – a one-point rise in unemployment goes with a fall of 0.00347 on a 0–1 framing scale
- **std.error** – how much that estimate would wobble across repeated samples
- **statistic** – the *t*: the estimate divided by its standard error. Roughly, how many standard errors from zero
- **p.value** – how often you would see a *t* this large if the true value were zero
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
`broom::tidy()` returns the table as a **data frame**, so you can filter it, join it, plot it. That is how 840 model fits become one chart this afternoon.
:::

::: notes
And what comes back. Broom's tidy function turns the model into a small table. The estimate says a one-point rise in the unemployment rate goes with a fall of about three thousandths on a nought-to-one framing scale – small, but the scale is small too, which is why we will standardise later. The standard error says how much that estimate would move across repeated samples. The statistic is the t: the estimate divided by its standard error, which you can read as how many standard errors the estimate sits from zero. And the p-value says how often you would see a t that large if the true value were zero. Now the fragment, which matters more than it looks: tidy hands the table back as a data frame. That means you can filter it, join it, stack hundreds of them and plot the lot – and that is precisely how eight hundred and forty model fits become one chart this afternoon.
:::

## One line of ggplot {.smaller .deepdive}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|2|3|4"}
ggplot(euframes, aes(x = year, y = mcosmo)) +   # data, and what maps to what
  geom_line(colour = "grey55") +                # draw lines
  geom_point(size = 0.7) +                      # and points
  facet_wrap(~ cntry)                           # one small panel per country
```

::: {.small}
Three parts, always: the **data**, the **mapping** (`aes`) from variables to visual properties, and one or more **geoms** that draw something. Layers stack with `+`.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
`facet_wrap` is the one worth stealing today: it repeats the whole plot once per group. Twenty-seven small country panels, one line of code, and you can *see* which countries move.
:::

::: notes
Plotting, briefly, because you will use it in the next task. Ggplot always has three parts. The data. The mapping – that is what aes does – saying which variable becomes which visual property, here year on the horizontal and cosmopolitan framing on the vertical. And then one or more geoms that actually draw something, stacked with plus signs: lines, then points on top. The one worth stealing today is on the fragment: facet-wrap repeats the entire plot once per group, so that single line gives you twenty-seven small country panels side by side. That is the plot you will make in the next task, and I want you to actually look at it rather than skip past it, because you can see with your eyes which countries move sharply around 2009 – and that is the variation the fixed-effects model is using.
:::

## A causal graph is a set of formulas {.smaller .deepdive}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1-4|2|3|6|7"}
dag <- dagify(
  framing ~ unemployment,          # unemployment -> framing
  framing ~ country + year,        # country and year -> framing
  unemployment ~ country + year,   # ... and -> unemployment
  exposure = "unemployment",
  outcome  = "framing")

adjustmentSets(dag)                # what must I control for?
```

::: {.small}
Each line is **one arrow, read outcome-first** – exactly the same convention as a model formula. Which means you can comment an arrow out with a `#` and the code still runs.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
`adjustmentSets()` reads the graph and tells you which variables close every back-door path. Change an arrow, rerun, and watch the answer change.
:::

::: notes
And the last piece, which is the one you use in this next task. A causal graph in R is just a set of formulas, and they follow exactly the same convention you already learned for models: outcome on the left, cause on the right. So the first line says unemployment points at framing. The second says country and year both point at framing. The third says they also both point at unemployment – which makes them common causes, which makes them confounders. Then you declare which node is the exposure and which is the outcome. The lovely part is on the fragment. Because each arrow is its own line, you can put a hash in front of one and the code still runs, so wiring your beliefs into the graph is literally a matter of commenting lines in and out. And adjustmentSets reads the finished graph and tells you which variables you must control for. Change an arrow, rerun it, watch the answer change.
:::

## When it breaks {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.small}
| What you see | What it usually means |
|---|---|
| `could not find function "feols"` | The package is not loaded – add `library(fixest)` above |
| `object 'euframes' not found` | You ran this chunk before the one that creates it – go back up and run in order |
| `object 'unemp_c' not found` | The column does not exist yet – you skipped the `mutate()` that makes it |
| `+` on the console, nothing happens | An unclosed bracket or quote. Press **Esc** and look for the missing `)` |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Read the error. R's messages are terse but almost always literally true – it is telling you the name of the thing it could not find.
:::

::: notes
Four errors, which between them will be about ninety per cent of what you hit today. "Could not find function" means the package is not loaded – add the library line above it. "Object euframes not found" means you ran a chunk before the one that creates the object, so go back up and run them in order, and this is the notebook trap I mentioned this morning. "Object unemp underscore c not found" means you skipped the mutate line that makes the column. And if the console is showing you a plus sign and nothing is happening, R thinks you have not finished the command – there is an unclosed bracket or quote somewhere. Press Escape and go looking for it. The general advice is on the fragment and it is the single most useful habit: read the error. R's messages are terse and unfriendly, but they are almost always literally true – it is telling you the exact name of the thing it could not find.
:::

## Task 2, in the analysts' own words {.smaller}

::: {.claimcard}
"Focus on the **'Cosmopolitan' dimension** for EU framing and on the **unemployment rate** as the independent variable; **disregard contextual variables**."
:::

::: {.small}
Three instructions. Everything else – estimator, sample, weighting, functional form, how you build the scale – was left to us.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
That is the design working as intended. Fix just enough to make the numbers comparable; leave the rest free, so that what remains is a measurement of **analytical variability itself**.
:::

::: notes
Here, word for word, is what task two told us to do. Focus on the cosmopolitan dimension as the outcome, use the unemployment rate as the independent variable, and disregard the contextual variables. Three instructions – that is the whole brief. Everything else was left open: which estimator, which sample, whether to weight, what functional form, and even how to build the cosmopolitan scale out of the underlying items. And that is the design working exactly as intended. Multi100 fixed just enough to make five numbers comparable, and deliberately left the rest free, so that what remained would be a measurement of analytical variability itself rather than of anything about the paper. It follows that everything they left open is a place where five competent people could legitimately part company. And they did.
:::

## What those three instructions assume {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- **'The cosmopolitan dimension'** assumes the five items form one scale, and that a mean of them is the right summary. A sum, a share, or a factor score would all be defensible
- **'The unemployment rate'** assumes the claim is carried by unemployment. The paper's own abstract says 'poor economic performances' – which also names GDP growth
- **'Disregard contextual variables'** removes the country-level controls. That buys comparability and gives up any defence against a time-varying confounder
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
None of these is wrong. Each one is a **decision**, made for you, that a different study could reasonably have made differently.
:::

::: notes
Now unpack those three instructions, because each carries an assumption. 'The cosmopolitan dimension' takes for granted that the five items – peace, democracy, freedom of movement, cultural diversity, a stronger voice in the world – form one scale, and that averaging them is the right summary. A sum would be defensible. So would a share, or a factor score. 'The unemployment rate' assumes the claim is carried by unemployment, but the paper's own abstract says 'poor economic performances', which just as clearly names GDP growth – and in Task 1, three of the five of us used a GDP measure rather than unemployment. And 'disregard contextual variables' strips out the country-level controls, which buys you comparability across analysts and gives up any defence against a confounder that varies over time. None of these is wrong. Each is a decision, made for you, that another study could reasonably have made differently.
:::

## One deviation, and a reason for it {.smaller}

::: {.small}
For the rest of today the rule is: **change one axis, hold the other seven at baseline.**

Baseline = the specification you just reproduced: `mcosmo` · gaussian · unemployment · raw · no copredictor · two-way FE · all years · unweighted.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Why one at a time? Because it makes the class chart **readable**. Every dot in the room differs from a common baseline in exactly one declared way, so when a dot moves you can say what moved it.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
And one convention binds everyone: **claim-alignment**. The negative framings are reverse-coded, 1 − y, so that 'supports the claim' reads as a negative sign whatever your outcome. Without it the class chart would straddle zero by construction and look like noise.
:::

::: notes
Two ground rules before you touch the menu. First, one deviation: change one axis and hold the other seven at the baseline, which is the specification you have just reproduced – cosmopolitan outcome, gaussian, unemployment raw, no copredictor, two-way fixed effects, all years, unweighted. That sounds restrictive, and it is deliberate, because it is what makes the class chart readable. Every dot in the room will differ from one common baseline in exactly one declared way, so when a dot sits somewhere surprising we can say what put it there. Second, a convention that binds everybody: claim-alignment. If your outcome is one of the negative framings, it gets reverse-coded – one minus the scale – so that supporting the claim reads as a negative sign for every outcome in the room. Without that, half the class would be above zero by construction and the chart would look like noise.
:::
