## Six ways to say 'EU framing' {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.skiplink}
[12 optional slides · skip to Hands-on 4 →](#hands-on-4-work-the-menu)
:::

::: {.small}
| Scale | Items | Claim predicts |
|---|---|---|
| `mcosmo` | peace · democracy · free movement · diversity · voice | negative |
| `mutil` | prosperity · social protection | negative |
| `mcomm` | unemployment · identity · crime · borders | **positive** |
| `mlib` | bureaucracy · waste of money | **positive** |
| `mpos` | all seven positive items | negative |
| `mneg` | all six negative items | **positive** |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The claim says "decrease positive dimensions" – `mpos` is the more literal reading, `mcosmo` is what was instructed. That one disagreement is worth roughly **half** the variance in the grid.
:::

::: notes
Start with the outcome, because it turns out to matter more than everything else combined. One survey question – what does the EU mean to you personally – with thirteen response options, which the paper sorts into four scales. Cosmopolitan: peace, democracy, free movement, diversity, a stronger voice in the world. Utilitarian: prosperity and social protection. Communitarian: unemployment, loss of identity, crime, border control. Libertarian: bureaucracy and waste of money. And then two composites, all the positive items and all the negative ones. Notice the third column, because it trips people up: for the negative framings the claim predicts a positive coefficient, not a negative one. And notice the fragment. The claim's own words are "decrease positive dimensions", which points at the composite rather than at cosmopolitan alone. That one disagreement is worth about half the variance in the entire grid.
:::

## Building a scale: mean, sum or share? {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.small}
Five binary items per respondent. Three defensible summaries:

- **Mean** of the five – a proportion between 0 and 1. Everyone contributes equally
- **Sum** – a count from 0 to 5. Same information, different scale, different coefficient size
- **Share** of all mentions – depends on how many options the respondent picked overall
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
These are not cosmetic. A **share** is relative to the respondent's own total, so somebody who ticked eight boxes contributes differently from somebody who ticked two. Mean and sum are not.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Among the five Multi100 analysts: one used a **mean**, one a **sum**, one a **share**, one three separate shares. All defensible; none the same quantity.
:::

::: notes
And how do you turn five binary items into one number? Three summaries, all defensible. The mean of the five, which gives you a proportion between nought and one and lets every item count equally – that is what our panel uses. The sum, which is a count from nought to five: the same information on a different scale, so the coefficient will be five times bigger and mean the same thing. Or a share of all the respondent's mentions, which is the interesting one, because it is relative to how many boxes that person ticked overall. Somebody who ticked eight options contributes differently from somebody who ticked two. The mean and the sum do not work that way. And look at the fragment: among the five of us, one used a mean, one a sum, one a share, one three separate shares. All defensible, and not one of them the same quantity as the others.
:::

## Claim alignment, and why the room needs it {.smaller .deepdive}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|3"}
d$mcomm_ca <- 1 - d$mcomm      # reverse-code a negative framing

# now: negative coefficient = supports the claim, whatever the outcome
```

::: {.small}
Reverse-coding a bounded scale **flips the sign** of *b*, *t* and *r*, and leaves the magnitude, the standard error, the |t| and the p-value untouched. Exactly so for the beta family too, since logit(1 − μ) = −logit(μ).
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Nothing about your evidence changes. Only the direction convention it is reported in.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
It is still a real analytic decision, which is why it rides on an explicit `claim_align` switch in your preregistration rather than sitting silently inside the fitting code.
:::

::: notes
Now the convention that makes the class chart work. If your outcome is one of the negative framings, you reverse-code it before fitting: one minus the scale. What that does is flip the sign of the coefficient, the t and the partial r, and leave everything else exactly where it was – the magnitude, the standard error, the absolute t, the p-value. And it holds exactly for the beta family too, because the logit of one minus mu is just minus the logit of mu. So nothing about your evidence changes; only the direction convention it is reported in. But – and this is why we do it explicitly – it is still a real analytic decision, and a reader deserves to see it. That is why it rides on a visible claim-align switch in your preregistration block rather than being buried three lines inside the fitting code where nobody would find it.
:::

## A bounded scale in a linear model {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.small}
Our outcome is a proportion: it lives strictly between 0 and 1, and its variance is smallest near the ends. A linear model assumes neither of those things.

- **Gaussian** – fit it as if it were unbounded. Simple, familiar, and can in principle predict outside 0–1
- **Beta** – a logit-link beta regression, built for exactly this shape. Reports a **z**, not a *t*
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
On this claim, the two agree: the beta twin of the baseline gives **b(logit) = −0.01399, z = −4.075, r = −0.258**, against the gaussian **r = −0.242**. Same direction, still significant, marginally stronger.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Which is worth knowing. The seminar argument about distributional assumptions is real, and on this claim it moves almost nothing.
:::

::: notes
Here is a proper methodological question. Our outcome is a proportion – it lives strictly between nought and one, and its variance is necessarily smallest near the two ends, because a mean near zero cannot vary much. A linear model assumes neither of those things. So you have a choice. Gaussian treats it as if it were unbounded: simple, familiar, and in principle capable of predicting a framing score of one point two. Or beta regression with a logit link, which is built for exactly this shape and reports a z rather than a t. Now the part I like. On this claim the two agree: the beta twin of our baseline gives a logit coefficient of minus point zero one four, z of minus four point zero eight, partial r of minus point two six, against the gaussian's minus point two four. Same direction, still significant, marginally stronger. The distributional argument is a real one, and here it moves almost nothing.
:::

## Which variable carries the claim? {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.small}
The abstract says "poor economic performances". That names at least two things:

- **Unemployment rate** – what Task 2 instructed. Higher is worse
- **GDP growth** – what three of the five analysts chose in their free phase. Higher is *better*, so the claim predicts a **positive** coefficient on positive framings
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Fitted on our panel, the growth mirror of the baseline gives **b = +0.00167, t = 1.59** – the right direction, not significant.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Across the whole growth half of the grid: **70.5%** in the claim's direction, but only **46.9%** significant. Direction without significance – a different kind of support from the unemployment story.
:::

::: notes
Which variable actually carries the claim? The abstract says "poor economic performances", and that phrase names at least two different things. The unemployment rate, which is what task two instructed and where higher means worse. Or GDP growth, which is what three of the five of us reached for when we were free to choose, and where higher means better – so the claim predicts a positive coefficient on the positive framings, not a negative one. Fit the growth mirror of our baseline on this panel and you get plus point zero zero one seven with a t of one point six: right direction, not significant. And across the whole growth half of the grid, seventy per cent in the claim's direction but only forty-seven per cent significant. That is direction without significance, which is a materially different kind of support from what the unemployment story offers, and a reader deserves to be told which one they are getting.
:::

## Predictor form, and a warning {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.small}
- **Raw** `unemp` – a one-point rise in the rate
- **log(unemp)** – a proportional rise. Says the step from 4% to 5% matters more than 20% to 21%
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Those two are genuinely different models and can give different answers.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
But **centring and standardising are not**. Subtracting a mean, or dividing by a standard deviation, is an *affine* change of scale: it moves the coefficient and its standard error by the same factor and leaves **t, r and p exactly unchanged**.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Which is why the grid holds no separate centred rows. If a robustness check varies only the centring, it is not a robustness check – it is the same analysis, restated.
:::

::: notes
Predictor form. Raw unemployment asks what a one-point rise in the rate does. Logged unemployment asks what a proportional rise does, which is a substantively different claim: it says the step from four per cent to five matters more than the step from twenty to twenty-one, and for something like unemployment that is quite plausible. Those two are genuinely different models and they can give different answers. But now the warning, and it is the single most useful thing on this slide. Centring and standardising are not. Subtracting a mean, or dividing by a standard deviation, is an affine change of scale: it moves the coefficient and its standard error by exactly the same factor, so the t, the partial r and the p-value are untouched. That is why our grid contains no separate centred rows at all. If you see a robustness check that varies only the centring, it is not a robustness check – it is the same analysis written differently.
:::

## Four ways to handle countries and years {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.small}
| Estimator | What it compares | What it assumes |
|---|---|---|
| **Pooled, clustered SE** | countries with each other *and* over time | no unobserved country differences |
| **Country FE** | each country with itself over time | country differences are stable |
| **Two-way FE** | the same, net of EU-wide year shocks | shocks hit everyone alike |
| **Random effects** | a weighted blend of both comparisons | country effects uncorrelated with the predictor |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
These do not answer the same question. Pooled asks whether *high-unemployment countries* frame the EU differently; fixed effects ask whether *a country frames it differently when its own rate rises*.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
And it shows: of the 41 wrong-sign specifications in the cosmopolitan universe, **33 are pooled**.
:::

::: notes
Four estimators, and the crucial thing is that they do not answer the same question. Pooled with clustered standard errors compares countries with each other and with themselves at once, and assumes there is nothing systematically different about countries that you have not measured – which for twenty-seven European states is a strong assumption. Country fixed effects compare each country only with itself over time, which means every stable national difference drops out. Two-way fixed effects do the same and additionally soak up anything that hit all of Europe in a given year. Random effects blend the two comparisons, weighting by precision, and assume the country effects are uncorrelated with your predictor. Read the fragment carefully, because this is the substantive point: pooled asks whether high-unemployment countries frame the EU differently, and fixed effects ask whether a country frames it differently when its own rate rises. Different questions. And it shows – thirty-three of the forty-one wrong-sign specifications are pooled.
:::

## What fixed effects actually buy you {.smaller .deepdive}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.small}
**They do absorb**

- Anything stable about a country over the decade – institutions, history, size, prior EU sentiment
- Anything common to a year across all countries – the crisis itself, a treaty, a media cycle
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.small}
**They do not touch**

- A confounder that **varies within a country over time** – a national bailout, a change of government
- **Reverse causation**: today's framing moving tomorrow's unemployment
- Measurement error, selection into the sample
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
This is the same statement as the DAG you drew before lunch. `adjustmentSets()` on the committed graph returns country and year – exactly what two-way fixed effects absorb. **The graph and the baseline model are one claim in two languages.**
:::

::: notes
Worth being precise about what fixed effects buy, because they are often treated as a general-purpose cure. They absorb anything stable about a country across the decade – institutions, history, size, whatever the country already thought about the EU in 2004. And they absorb anything common to a year across all countries: the crisis itself, a treaty, a Europe-wide media cycle. What they do not touch is anything that varies within a country over time, which is precisely where the interesting confounders live – a national bailout programme, a change of government, a domestic scandal. They do nothing about reverse causation, where today's framing moves tomorrow's unemployment. And nothing about measurement error or selection. And here is the pleasing part on the fragment: run adjustmentSets on the graph you built before lunch and it returns country and year. The graph and the baseline model are the same claim written in two languages.
:::

## Copredictor: control, or second exposure? {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.small}
Put GDP growth in beside unemployment and you have made a choice you should be able to name:

- **As a confounder** – a slump raises unemployment *and* sours sentiment in the same year. Adjusting closes a back-door your fixed effects cannot reach
- **As a rival exposure** – growth is a second measure of the same "poor economic performance". Now you are asking which one carries the claim
- **As a mediator** – if unemployment works *through* growth, adjusting removes part of the effect you wanted
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Same line of code, three different estimands. And remember the **Table 2 fallacy**: the growth coefficient in that model is not automatically the causal effect of growth.
:::

::: notes
The copredictor axis looks like the most innocuous choice on the menu and is quietly the most treacherous. If you put GDP growth into the model beside unemployment, you have made a choice, and you should be able to say which one. You might mean it as a confounder: a slump raises unemployment and sours sentiment in the same year, so adjusting for growth closes a back-door path that your fixed effects cannot reach, because it varies within country over time. Or you might mean it as a rival exposure – growth is another measure of the same poor economic performance, and you are now asking which of them carries the claim. Or, if unemployment works partly through growth, growth is a mediator and adjusting for it removes part of the very effect you set out to measure. Same line of code, three different estimands. And do not forget the Table 2 fallacy: the growth coefficient in that model is not automatically the causal effect of growth.
:::

## Sample: which countries, which years {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.small}
- **All** – 2004–2013, 27 countries, 270 cells
- **2004–2008** vs **2009–2013** – before and during. Halves your data and asks whether the relationship is a crisis phenomenon
- **No bailout countries** – drop the cells where an EU/IMF programme was running
- **No Greece and Spain** – drop the two extreme unemployment trajectories
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The last two are the interesting ones. If the association is carried by a handful of extreme cases, removing them should worry you – and it does something visible here: **24 of the 41 wrong-sign specifications** sit in bailout-excluding samples.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
An exclusion is a claim about **who the finding is meant to be about**. That is an estimand question, not a housekeeping one.
:::

::: notes
Sample. All years is the baseline. Splitting into 2004 to 2008 and 2009 to 2013 halves your data and asks a real question: is this a crisis phenomenon or a standing relationship? Then two exclusions. Drop the countries while an EU or IMF programme was running. Or drop Greece and Spain, whose unemployment trajectories are so extreme they could plausibly drive the whole thing on their own. Those last two are the interesting ones, because if an association is carried by a handful of extreme cases, taking them out should worry you – and it does something visible here: twenty-four of the forty-one wrong-sign specifications sit in bailout-excluding samples. Take the crisis countries out and the association goes. And notice what an exclusion really is. It is a claim about who your finding is meant to be about. That makes it an estimand question, not housekeeping.
:::

## Weights: whose country-year counts more? {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.small}
Each cell is a mean of very different numbers of respondents. Weighting by `n_cy` says a cell built from 2,000 people should count more than one built from 500.

- **Unweighted** – every country-year is one observation. You are studying *countries*
- **Weighted by `n_cy`** – cells count in proportion to the people behind them. You are closer to studying *people*
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
That is a shift of estimand, not a technical refinement. Which is why the day's convention is to declare it.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Practical note: random effects are never fitted with weights in the grid – the combination is not well defined for this design, so those rows do not exist.
:::

::: notes
Weights. Each cell in the panel is a mean over a very different number of respondents, so weighting by that count says a country-year built from two thousand people should carry more than one built from five hundred. And that sounds like a purely technical refinement, but it is not. Unweighted, every country-year is one observation and you are studying countries – Malta counts as much as Germany. Weighted, cells count in proportion to the people behind them, and you have moved a long way towards studying people. That is a change of estimand, not a change of estimator, which is exactly why the day's convention is that you declare it rather than let it sit in an argument to the fitting function. One practical note: random effects are never fitted with weights in our grid, because the combination is not well defined for this design, so those rows simply do not exist.
:::

## Making eight axes comparable {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.small}
A coefficient from a beta model on a share and one from a weighted pooled model on a sum are not on the same scale. Multi100's answer, and ours:

- Take the test statistic and its degrees of freedom
- Convert to a **partial correlation** *r* – the association between predictor and outcome, net of everything else in the model, on a fixed −1 to +1 scale
- Apply **claim alignment**, so the sign means the same thing everywhere
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Now every specification in the room, and all 840 in the grid, sit on one axis. `report_result()` does the conversion for you.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The cost is worth naming: standardising makes numbers **comparable**, not **equivalent**. It cannot rescue two analyses that estimate different quantities – it can only put them side by side.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Silberzahn's teams hit the same wall: four of the twenty-nine reported a correlation or a standardised difference rather than an odds ratio. The authors converted everything to one scale and reported the **median**. That is a different answer to the same problem – a median is one number, a curve is a distribution – and which you want depends on what you mean to say next.
:::

::: notes
Last one, and it is what makes the afternoon possible. A coefficient from a beta model on a share and a coefficient from a weighted pooled model on a sum are simply not on the same scale – you cannot put them on one axis and read anything off it. Multi100's answer, and ours, is to take the test statistic and its degrees of freedom, convert to a partial correlation, and then apply claim alignment so the sign means the same thing everywhere. A partial r is the association between predictor and outcome net of everything else in the model, on a fixed scale from minus one to plus one. Report underscore result does that conversion for you. And the cost deserves naming: standardising makes numbers comparable, not equivalent. It cannot rescue two analyses that are estimating different quantities. All it can do is put them next to each other – which is exactly what Part 2 warned you about.
:::

## You just built a small multiverse {.smaller}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
You ran three or four specifications, all defensible, and watched the estimate move.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Nothing about that is unusual. **Every analysis you have ever published sat inside a space like that** – you simply reported one point from it.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The multiverse idea is not a new estimator. It is the proposal that the **space** is the finding, and that showing one point without it is a form of incomplete reporting.
:::
::::

::: notes
Look at what you just did. You ran three or four specifications, every one of them defensible, and you watched the estimate move around. Now – nothing about that is unusual or improper. I want to say that clearly, because there is a slightly accusatory tone in some of this literature that I do not think is deserved. Every analysis any of us has ever published sat inside a space exactly like the one you were just wandering around in. The difference is that we reported one point from it and did not mention the rest, mostly because it did not occur to us that the rest was reportable. So the multiverse idea is not a new estimator and not an accusation. It is the proposal that the space itself is a finding, and that showing one point from it without the space around it is a form of incomplete reporting.
:::

<!-- DEEP DIVE START: multiverse tutorial (8 slides). To skip it on the day,
     comment out the region between this marker and DEEP DIVE END. -->

## Where the idea comes from {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.skiplink}
[8 optional slides · skip to the class chart →](#the-class-multiverse)
:::

::: {.small}
- **Multiverse analysis** [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse] – born from *data-processing* choices: how you code, exclude and combine. Report the whole set of datasets your choices could have produced
- **Specification curve analysis** [@SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis] – the same move for *model* choices, plus a visual grammar: estimates on top, the choices that produced each one underneath
- **The vibration of effects** – the same idea, arrived at independently in epidemiology
- **The book-length treatment** [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational] – computational recipes at scale
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Different names, one move: **stop treating your analytical choices as invisible, and enumerate them.**
:::

::: notes
Brief history, because the vocabulary is a mess and knowing which word came from where helps. Multiverse analysis is Steegen and colleagues in 2016, and it grew out of data-processing choices specifically – how you code a variable, which cases you exclude, how you combine items – with the proposal that you report the whole set of datasets your choices could have produced. Specification curve analysis is Simonsohn, Simmons and Nelson, making the same move for model choices, and adding the visual grammar you are about to see: estimates plotted on top, and underneath them a panel showing which choices produced each one. The vibration of effects is the same idea arrived at independently in epidemiology, which tells you it is a natural response to the problem rather than a fashion. And there is now a book-length treatment with computational recipes. Different names, one move: stop treating your analytical choices as invisible and enumerate them.
:::

## The garden, drawn {.smaller .deepdive}

```{r}
#| label: forking-paths
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.6
# A binary decision tree over four choices: 16 end points, one path highlighted.
# Drawn from coordinates rather than data - this is an illustration of the
# structure of a decision sequence, not a result.
lev <- 4
seg <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(lev), function(k) {
  n_parent <- 2^(k - 1)
  purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(n_parent), function(j) {
    y0 <- (j - 0.5) / n_parent
    tibble::tibble(
      x = k - 1, xend = k,
      y = y0,
      yend = c(y0 - 0.5 / 2^k, y0 + 0.5 / 2^k),
      lit = k <= 1 | FALSE)
  })
})
# Highlight one route through the tree: always the upper branch.
route <- tibble::tibble(x = 0:3, xend = 1:4,
                        y = c(0.5, 0.75, 0.875, 0.9375),
                        yend = c(0.75, 0.875, 0.9375, 0.96875))

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = seg, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               colour = "#c7ccd2", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_segment(data = route, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
               colour = d_red, linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = 0:3 + 0.5, y = -0.06,
           label = c("outcome", "estimator", "sample", "weights"),
           colour = ncl_blue, fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 4.05, y = 0.96875, hjust = 0,
           label = "the one you published",
           colour = d_red, fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 5.6), ylim = c(-0.1, 1.05), clip = "off") +
  theme_void()
```

::: {.small}
Four binary choices give sixteen analyses. **Eight axes with several options each give hundreds.** The published paper reports one red line and no tree.
:::

::: notes
Here is the structure of the problem, drawn. Four choices, two options each, and you already have sixteen distinct analyses. Our menu has eight axes and most of them have more than two options, which is how you get to hundreds. And the point of the picture is the red line: what a published paper reports is one route through this tree, with no indication that the tree exists. The reader sees a coefficient and a standard error, and the standard error describes uncertainty from sampling – it says nothing whatever about the fifteen other branches. Gelman and Loken's phrase for this is the garden of forking paths, and their sharp observation, which we met this morning, is that you do not have to walk every path for this to be a problem. Walking one path that you chose after seeing the data is enough.
:::

## Justifiable, not merely possible {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.small}
A multiverse is **not** every analysis you could run. Two filters have to be applied before anything goes in:

- **Justifiability** – could you defend this specification to a reviewer, in writing, before seeing its result?
- **The same estimand** – does it estimate the quantity you said you were after?
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Drop the first filter and you get a cloud of nonsense that makes any finding look fragile. Drop the second and you are averaging over answers to different questions – which is the red-card mistake, at scale.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Today's grid is a **curated 840**, chosen against both filters. That curation is itself an analytical decision, and it is the one a critic should attack first.
:::

::: notes
Now the most important slide in this run, because it is where multiverse analysis is most often done badly. A multiverse is not every analysis you could run. Two filters have to be applied before a specification is allowed in. The first is justifiability: could you defend this specification to a reviewer, in writing, before seeing what it gives? The second is that it has to estimate the same quantity you said you were after. Drop the first filter and you generate a cloud of nonsense, and since nonsense specifications produce scattered answers, any finding on earth looks fragile. Drop the second and you are averaging over answers to different questions, which is the red-card mistake reproduced at scale. Today's grid is a curated eight hundred and forty, chosen against both filters. And notice that the curation is itself an analytical decision – it is the first thing a critic should attack.
:::

## Enumerate, or curate? {.smaller .deepdive}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**Enumerate**

Cross every option on every axis. Complete, mechanical, reproducible.

Risk: the set fills up with specifications nobody would defend, and the spread stops meaning anything.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**Curate**

Include only the specifications you would actually defend.

Risk: you are choosing the set, so a sceptic can ask whether you chose it to get the picture you wanted.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
There is no way out of this. Either way, **the set is a claim**, and it belongs in the paper alongside the curve – ideally declared before the curve is drawn.
:::

::: notes
So how do you build the set? Two strategies, and both have a real cost. Enumerate: cross every option on every axis mechanically. It is complete, it is reproducible, and nobody can accuse you of hand-picking. The risk is that the set fills up with specifications nobody would defend, and once it does, the spread stops meaning anything – of course the answer varies, you included analyses that are wrong. Or curate: include only the specifications you would actually defend in print. That fixes the first problem and creates a second, because now you are choosing the set, and a sceptic can reasonably ask whether you chose it to produce the picture you wanted. There is no way out of this dilemma, and I do not think you should pretend there is. Either way the set is a claim, it belongs in the paper next to the curve, and ideally it is declared before the curve is drawn.
:::

## The arithmetic gets away from you {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.small}
Our menu, multiplied out:

- 6 outcomes × 2 predictor forms × 3 copredictors × 4 estimators × 5 samples × 2 weightings, minus the combinations that are not defined → **840** distinct analyses
- Add the **outcome family** axis → **1,680**
- Add **GDP growth** as the claim carrier → **2,520**
- Open the **unit of analysis** as well – person level or aggregate – and the menu arithmetic runs past **5,000**
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Two consequences. **Compute stops being free**, so somebody must decide what is worth running. And **you cannot look at 2,520 numbers** – you need a picture, and a way to ask which axis is doing the work.
:::

::: notes
And here is what happens when you multiply the menu out. Six outcomes, two predictor forms, three copredictor settings, four estimators, five samples, two weightings – minus the combinations that are not defined, like random effects with weights – and you land on eight hundred and forty distinct analyses. Add the outcome family axis and it doubles to one thousand six hundred and eighty. Add GDP growth as an alternative claim carrier and it is two and a half thousand. And if you also opened the unit of analysis, person level or aggregate, the menu arithmetic runs past five thousand. Two consequences follow. First, compute stops being free, so somebody has to decide what is worth running, and that decision is not neutral. Second, and more practically, you cannot look at two and a half thousand numbers. You need a picture, and you need a way of asking which axis is actually doing the work.
:::

## What is a multiverse *for*? {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.small}
Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman's question, and it has three different answers that want three differently built universes:

- **Reflection** – to understand your own analysis. Which choices matter, where the argument has to happen. Build it broad, and read it yourself
- **Persuasion** – to convince a reader the finding is not an artefact of one path. Build it from specifications *your critic* would accept
- **Inference** – to make a probabilistic statement about the curve as a whole. Build it to a fixed, declared rule, and bring a null distribution
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Today's grid was built for **reflection**. Reading it as inference is the mistake we spend the next four slides avoiding.
:::

::: {.src}
@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood
:::

::: notes
And then the question that organises the whole debate, which is Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman's: what is a multiverse actually for? Because there are three answers and they want three differently built universes. If it is for reflection – understanding your own analysis, finding out which choices matter and where the argument has to happen – build it broad and read it yourself; it does not even have to go in the paper. If it is for persuasion – convincing a reader that your finding is not an artefact of one path – then build it out of specifications your critic would accept, not ones you like. And if it is for inference, making a probabilistic statement about the curve as a whole, then you need a fixed declared rule and a null distribution, and that is a much heavier undertaking. Today's grid was built for reflection. Reading it as inference is exactly the mistake the next few slides are about avoiding.
:::

## Which fork matters? {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.small}
Once you have hundreds of estimates and the choices that produced each one, you can ask a question no single analysis can answer: **how much of the variation does each axis account for?**

- Treat the specification grid as data: one row per analysis, the axes as factors, the estimate as the outcome
- Decompose the variance across axes
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The answer is the most useful thing a multiverse produces, because it tells you **where to spend your argument**. An axis that moves nothing does not need defending. An axis that moves everything needs a paragraph.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
On this claim, the answer surprises almost everybody – which is why you are going to bet on it in a minute before I show you.
:::

::: notes
Here is the analysis that only becomes possible once you have hundreds of estimates and a record of which choices produced each one. You can turn the grid itself into a dataset – one row per analysis, the eight axes as factors, the estimate as the outcome – and decompose the variance across axes. How much of the spread does each fork account for? I think that is the most useful thing a multiverse produces, and it is much more useful than the curve itself, because it tells you where to spend your argument. An axis that moves nothing does not need defending in your paper; you can say so in a sentence and move on. An axis that moves everything needs a paragraph of justification, and probably a sensitivity analysis. On this claim the answer surprises nearly everybody, which is why in a moment I am going to make you bet on it before I show you.
:::

## Reading a specification curve {.smaller .deepdive}

::: {.small}
Five questions to ask any curve you meet, in any paper:

1. **What is on the vertical axis** – a raw coefficient, or something standardised? Are the signs aligned so that up and down mean the same thing throughout?
2. **How was the set built** – enumerated or curated, and by whom?
3. **Where does the published estimate sit** – at the median, or out at an end?
4. **Is the spread patterned** – does one axis produce the extremes, or is it scattered?
5. **What null is the significance shading against** – and are the specifications independent? (They almost never are.)
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
You are about to answer all five for your own curve. That is a publishable robustness section.
:::

::: notes
And to close the tutorial, five questions to ask of any specification curve you ever meet, in anybody's paper. One: what is on the vertical axis – a raw coefficient, which is not comparable across outcomes, or something standardised; and are the signs aligned so that up and down mean the same thing all the way across. Two: how was the set built, enumerated or curated, and by whom. Three: where does the published estimate sit – comfortably at the median, or out at one end, because those are very different situations for the author. Four: is the spread patterned – does one axis produce all the extremes, or is it genuinely scattered. And five, the one nobody asks: what null is that significance shading against, and are the specifications independent of each other? They almost never are, and we will spend some time on why that matters. You are about to answer all five for your own curve, and that is a publishable robustness section.
:::

## The outcome fork carries half of everything

```{r}
#| label: fork-importance
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
# Share of specification variance in partial r per menu axis, from the
# facilitator's extended decomposition (data/fork_importance.csv, main-effects
# eta-squared). Bars ordered by share; the outcome fork in orange.
fi <- fork_imp |>
  dplyr::mutate(axis = dplyr::recode(term,
    outcome   = "outcome",
    Residuals = "residual / interactions",
    sample    = "sample",
    estimator = "estimator",
    exposure  = "predictor form",
    control   = "copredictor",
    weights   = "weights")) |>
  dplyr::arrange(share) |>
  dplyr::mutate(axis = factor(axis, levels = axis))
ggplot(fi, aes(share, axis, fill = axis == "outcome")) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", share)),
            hjust = -0.15, colour = ncl_blue, fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = orange, `FALSE` = ncl_blue),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 60)) +
  labs(x = "share of variance in partial r (%)", y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(16)
```

::: {.small}
- **Outcome operationalisation: 49.7%** of specification variance · estimator + predictor form + copredictor + weights together: **under 2%**
- Computed on the grid **as estimated** – part of the outcome share *is* the polarity split between positive and negative framings, the split the claim-aligned chart removes from display
:::

::: {.src}
Computed over the committed data/spec_grid.csv; imported as data/fork_importance.csv.
:::

::: notes
The outcome fork carries essentially half of all the variation in the grid – forty-nine point seven per cent. And now look at the bottom of the chart: estimator, predictor form, copredictor and weights – the axes we argue about in seminars – together account for under two per cent. The residual block is interactions, combinations that matter beyond any single axis. One caveat, stated plainly: this decomposition is computed on the grid as estimated, before claim-alignment, so part of the outcome fork's share is the polarity split itself – positive framings falling, negative framings rising. That split is real variation in what the specifications estimate; the aligned chart removes it from the display, not from the decomposition. So the day's empirical lesson stands: *what you measure* dwarfs *how you model it*. The fixed-versus-random-effects debate, the to-weight-or-not debate – on this claim, they barely move the needle. Deciding what 'EU framing' means moves it half the distance all by itself. Whoever guessed "outcome" in the chat: take the point.
:::

:::

::: notes
Now put the five published analysts inside the same grid – for each one, the share of all eight hundred and forty claim-aligned specifications that come out more negative than their value. And look who sits at the ends. KEVF1, the most strongly claim-supporting of the five at around the sixteenth percentile, and PRL47, the closest to the null at around the sixty-eighth – those two, at the opposite extremes, are the two analysts who worked at *person level*, on the third of a million respondents, rather than on aggregates. The three aggregate pipelines sit between them; my own constrained baseline lands almost exactly at the grid's median. It is not Stata versus R, and it is not the estimator: it is the unit of analysis and the outcome metric, decided before any model is fitted, that scatter five competent people across half the curve. Which is the fork-importance chart again, wearing faces.
:::

## The sign flips are patterned, not random

```{r}
#| label: sign-flips
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.8
# Wrong-sign (positive) estimates in the cosmopolitan-only universe,
# cross-tabbed by estimator and by sample; computed in-chunk from the
# committed spec_grid.csv (flips_mcosmo in the setup chunk).
f_est <- flips_mcosmo |>
  dplyr::count(estimator, wrong_sign) |>
  dplyr::filter(wrong_sign) |>
  dplyr::arrange(n) |>
  dplyr::mutate(estimator = factor(estimator, levels = estimator))
f_smp <- flips_mcosmo |>
  dplyr::count(sample, wrong_sign) |>
  dplyr::filter(wrong_sign) |>
  dplyr::arrange(n) |>
  dplyr::mutate(sample = factor(sample, levels = sample))
p_est <- ggplot(f_est, aes(n, estimator)) +
  geom_col(fill = d_red, width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.3, colour = ncl_blue,
            fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.2))) +
  labs(x = "wrong-sign specs", y = NULL, title = "by estimator") +
  theme_slide(14)
p_smp <- ggplot(f_smp, aes(n, sample)) +
  geom_col(fill = d_red, width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.3, colour = ncl_blue,
            fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.2))) +
  labs(x = "wrong-sign specs", y = NULL, title = "by sample") +
  theme_slide(14)
p_est + p_smp
```

::: {.small}
- In the cosmopolitan-only universe, the wrong-sign estimates concentrate in the **pooled cluster-robust estimator** and the **bailout-excluding samples**
:::

::: notes
One more way to read the grid: where do the sign flips live? Take only the cosmopolitan-outcome specifications – the claim predicts a negative coefficient, so a positive estimate is a flip – and cross-tab the flips by axis. They are not scattered randomly. The estimator that absorbs no between-country differences at all – the pooled model with clustered errors – hosts thirty-three of the forty-one, and the flips also lean heavily towards the samples that exclude the bailout countries. In other words, when this claim flips sign, it flips for identifiable, diagnosable reasons: remove the between-country comparison, or remove the crisis countries, and the association goes. A specification curve is not just a spread to gawp at – it has anatomy, and you can dissect it.
:::

## What the curve leaves out {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- **The specifications nobody ran.** Person-level models, a different scale construction, a lagged predictor. The curve is silent about everything outside the menu, and looks just as complete either way
- **The dependence.** All 840 use the same 270 country-years, so they share their noise. The width of the cloud is not 840 independent opinions
- **Estimand drift.** Some of these specifications answer subtly different questions. The chart puts them on one axis; that does not make them commensurable
- **The data-building choices.** Everything upstream of the panel – how the scales were coded, which waves were pooled – is fixed for everyone here
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
A curve is a **map of the menu you wrote**. It cannot tell you the menu was the right one.
:::

::: notes
Before we go on, four things this picture does not contain, because a chart this satisfying invites you to think it is complete. First, the specifications nobody ran: person-level models, a different scale construction, a lagged predictor. The curve is silent about everything outside the menu, and – this is the treacherous part – it looks exactly as complete either way. Second, the dependence: all eight hundred and forty of these use the same two hundred and seventy country-years, so they share their noise, and the width of that cloud is not eight hundred and forty independent opinions. Third, estimand drift: some of these answer subtly different questions, and putting them on one axis does not make them commensurable. And fourth, everything upstream of the panel – how the scales were coded, which waves were pooled – is fixed for everyone in this room. A curve is a map of the menu you wrote, and it cannot tell you the menu was right.
:::

## Two jobs, one curve

::: {.none}
**Description** – map how the estimate moves across every defensible choice. *(What we have been doing all day.)*

::: {.fragment}
**Inference** – ask whether the curve *as a whole* is surprising if there were no effect at all. *(A different, harder job.)*
:::

::: {.fragment}
The two are detachable, and most published curves stop at description.
:::
:::

::: {.src}
@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse; @SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis
:::

::: notes
Last conceptual move of the day, and it is the one that separates careful readers of specification curves from impressed ones. A curve like ours does two different jobs. The first is description: showing how the estimate moves as the choices move – that is what we built, and it is genuinely valuable on its own. The second is inference: asking whether the curve, taken as a whole, is more extreme than you would expect if there were no effect at all. Those are different questions with different machinery, and they detach cleanly – Multi100 did the description without the inference, and so, so far, have we. The next three slides are about what the second job takes.
:::

## 840 estimates are not 840 tests

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
Every specification re-uses the **same 270 country-years**. The estimates are deeply dependent.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
'63.9% significant' **describes** the curve. It is not a p-value for the claim.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
Vote-counting across dependent specifications has no null distribution. You cannot tally the stars.
:::
::::

::: notes
Here is the trap the percentages set. Sixty-three point nine per cent of our specifications are significant. It is very tempting to read that as evidence strength: "most tests pass, so the claim holds". But all eight hundred and forty specifications interrogate the same two hundred and seventy country-years. They share the data, so they share the noise: if sampling luck pushed a handful of country-years the claim's way, it pushed hundreds of specifications the same way at once. The percentage significant is a description of the curve, not a test of the claim. To test the claim at curve level you need to know what the whole curve would look like if there were nothing to find – and that requires building the nothing.
:::

## Building the nothing: the permutation design

::: {.small}
- Break the one link the claim needs: **shuffle each country's unemployment series in time** (jointly with growth), keeping everything else intact
- Refit **all 840 specifications** on each shuffled dataset · repeat **B = 500** times
- Compare the observed curve to the 500 null curves: is ours more extreme than chance produces?
:::

::: {.src}
The design is worked through in your inference reading; permutation inference after @PhipsonSmyth2010PermutationPValues.
:::

::: notes
The nothing is built like this. The claim says a country's unemployment moves its EU framing over time. So take each country and shuffle its unemployment series in time – together with growth, so the macro side stays internally coherent – while leaving the framing data untouched. In a shuffled world the alignment between unemployment and framing is broken by construction: whatever curve you get is what pure chance produces on these exact data with these exact 840 specifications. Do that five hundred times, refit the entire grid each time, and you have five hundred ghost curves to stand ours against. If our curve sits in the far tail of those ghosts, the curve as a whole is evidence. If it sits comfortably among them – the description stands, but the inference does not.
:::

## How to read a curve-level test {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- With B = 500, the smallest reportable p is **2/(B+1) ≈ 0.004** – a floor, not a zero
- Near p = .05 the Monte-Carlo wobble is about **±0.01**, so treat p = .04 and p = .06 as the same finding
- [A DESIGN · NOT YET RUN]{.highlight bg-colour="#ffe3b3"} – a curve-level test has to be fixed in advance, and this one has not been run; today we read the design, not a result
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Discussion (2 minutes, then chat):** the constrained cosmopolitan-only universe has 140 specs: **70.7% negative, 57.1% negative *and* significant.** Strong evidence? *Against what null?*
:::

::: notes
Two literacy points and then you argue. First: with five hundred draws, the smallest p-value the test can report is two over five hundred and one – about point zero zero four. That is a resolution floor, not a zero; more draws buy sharper floors at real compute cost. Second: near the point-oh-five boundary the Monte-Carlo wobble is around plus or minus point zero one, so a permutation p of point zero four and point zero six are the same finding twice. And the badge matters: this test is designed, not run – you are reading a plan today, which is itself the preregistration lesson again. Now the discussion beat. The constrained universe – cosmopolitan outcome only, 140 specifications – is 70.7 per cent negative, 57.1 per cent negative and significant. Two minutes: is that strong evidence? Against what null? Type your answer. [harvest: the sharp ones will say – we don't know until we know what chance produces on these dependent data; that is exactly the point.]
:::

## What stands without the test

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
Everything descriptive survives: the **49.7%** outcome fork, the analysts' placement, the sign-flip anatomy, **your dot**.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
What waits for the permutation is one sentence: "the curve as a whole is unlikely under no effect".
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
Careful reporting says which of the two layers a claim lives in.
:::
::::

::: notes
So that nothing feels deflated: notice how much of today needs no permutation at all. That the outcome fork carries half the variance – description, stands. That the two person-level analysts bracket the range – stands. That the sign flips concentrate in the pooled estimator and the non-bailout samples – stands. The correction arc, your preregistered dot, the whole anatomy of the curve – all of it stands. The single sentence that has to wait is "this curve as a whole is unlikely if there is no effect". Keeping those two layers apart in your own writing – saying which one your claim lives in – puts you ahead of most published specification curves. That is inference literacy, and you now have it.
:::

## The multiverse has its critics {.smaller}

::: {.small}
- "Robustness is better assessed with a **few thoughtful models** than with billions of regressions" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed; answering @GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources] – only *justified* models targeting the *same estimand* belong in one curve. Today's grid is a **curated 840**, not billions, and the fork chart does the job every critic endorses: it locates where the argument must happen
- "**There is only one correct analysis**" once the question is fully specified [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne] – your declared specification answers *cherry-picking*, and their deeper point is that declaring in advance does not yet make a choice *justified*, which is what the estimand and DAG work were for
- "What's a multiverse **good for** anyway?" – reflection, persuasion, or inference, and each purpose wants a *differently built* universe [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood]. Today's was built for **reflection**, and how much more to read into it is the open debate
:::

::: {.src}
The book-length how-to: @YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational; the estimand diagnosis behind Part 2: @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial.
:::

::: notes
One last literacy layer: the method you practised is under live debate, and you can now read it. Katrin Auspurg – Part 2's estimand diagnosis – answered a 3.6-billion-estimate study with the line at the top of this slide: only thoughtful, justified models belong in a curve. Today mostly agreed with her: our grid is a curated eight hundred and forty, not an enumeration, and the fork chart does the one job every critic endorses – it tells you where the argument has to happen. Lakens and colleagues say that once the question is fixed, only one analysis implements it correctly. Your preregistration answered cherry-picking; their deeper point – that declaring early does not make a choice justified – is exactly why we built the DAG before declaring. And Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman ask what a multiverse is for: reflection, persuasion, or inference – each wanting a differently built set. Ours was built for reflection. How much more to read into it is the debate you have now joined. [advance]
:::

## "There is only one correct analysis" {.smaller}

::: {.small}
Lakens and colleagues push back hard, and the argument deserves to be taken seriously:

- A research question, **fully specified**, implies a quantity to be estimated
- That quantity, together with the design and the assumptions you are willing to make, implies **one analysis** that estimates it
- So a spread of results is not evidence of legitimate diversity. It is evidence that **most of those specifications are wrong** – they estimate something else
- On this reading, showing a wide curve is closer to an admission than to a robustness check
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Take it back to the red cards. Twenty-nine teams modelled one count of red cards as **linear, logistic or Poisson**. Those are claims about how the outcome was generated, and they cannot all be right – so on this argument the spread is not diversity, it is mostly error.
:::

::: {.src}
@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne
:::

::: notes
And now the strongest objection to everything I have just taught you, and I want to give it its full force rather than a straw version. Lakens and colleagues argue that a research question, once fully specified, implies a quantity to be estimated. That quantity, together with your design and the assumptions you are prepared to make, implies one analysis that estimates it. Not a family, one. From which it follows that a spread of results is not evidence of legitimate analytical diversity at all. It is evidence that most of those specifications are simply wrong – they estimate something other than what you said you wanted. And on that reading, publishing a wide specification curve is closer to an admission that you never specified your question than to a robustness check. That is an uncomfortable argument and I think it is largely right.
:::

## How would you know? {.smaller}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Grant the argument. **One correct analysis exists.** Now: which one is it?
:::

::: {.fragment}
Getting there needs the estimand *and* the identification assumptions *and* agreement about the measurement – and on this claim, reasonable people disagree about all three.
:::

::: {.fragment}
So the curve is not a rival to the one-correct-analysis view. It is a **map of the remaining disagreement**, drawn because we cannot yet settle it.
:::

::: {.fragment}
And it points at what to argue about: on this claim, at the **outcome**, not at the estimator.
:::
::::

::: notes
So let us grant the argument. Suppose one correct analysis does exist. The immediately following question is: which one is it, and how would you know? To get there you need the estimand, and the identification assumptions, and agreement about how the construct is measured – and on this claim reasonable people disagree about all three, as you saw for yourselves this afternoon. So I do not think the curve is a rival to the one-correct-analysis view at all. I think it is a map of the disagreement that remains, drawn precisely because we cannot yet settle it. And read that way it is genuinely useful, because it tells you where the disagreement lives. On this claim it lives at the outcome – what 'EU framing' means – and not at the estimator, which is where the seminar argument would have been.
:::

## What preregistration settles {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**It does settle**

- That your specification was not chosen *because of* the result
- That your rule for what counts as support was written before you had one
- That a reader can see what you intended, and what you changed
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**It does not settle**

- Whether the specification was **any good**
- Whether it estimates the quantity your question implies
- Whether the assumptions behind it hold

A badly-reasoned analysis declared in advance is still badly reasoned – now with a timestamp
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
Which is why the estimand and the DAG came **first** today. Preregistration protects a choice; it is the causal reasoning that makes the choice worth protecting.
:::

::: notes
So where does preregistration fit? It settles a specific and limited set of things, and the two columns matter equally. On the left: it settles that your specification was not chosen because of the result it gave, that your rule for what counts as support was written before you had a result to bend it around, and that a reader can see both what you intended and what you subsequently changed. Those are real guarantees and no other mechanism provides them. On the right, what it emphatically does not settle: whether the specification was any good, whether it estimates the quantity your question implies, or whether its assumptions hold. A badly reasoned analysis declared in advance is still badly reasoned – it just has a timestamp on it now. Which is exactly why we did the estimand and the graph first this morning. Preregistration protects a choice. Causal reasoning is what makes the choice worth protecting.
:::
## You are Analyst no. 6 – for real this time {.smaller}

::: {.big}
- Aim 2: assess the **robustness** of the constrained result
:::

::: {.small}
  - **Before the break** you explored: several specifications, tried in order to find out what they do. That was the right way to learn them

  - **Now** you commit: **one** specification, declared in writing *before* it runs, with a reason your DAG can carry

  - **The difference is not the code.** It is that one of these can be chosen because of its result and the other cannot
:::

::: notes
This afternoon you reproduced my constrained result, and then you explored – several specifications, tried in whatever order took your interest, in order to find out what they do. That was exactly the right way to learn them, and I want to be clear that there was nothing improper about it. Now comes the other half. You commit to one specification, declared in writing before it runs, with a reason your causal graph can carry. And notice what the difference between the two activities is, because it is not the code – the code is identical. The difference is that one of them can be chosen because of the result it gave, and the other one cannot. That is the whole distinction, and almost no published paper tells you which of the two it is reporting.
:::

## Every reanalysis leaves a public trail

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
**OSF**, the Open Science Framework: a timestamped, citable, public home for data, code, and **registrations**.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
A registration is a **frozen, dated snapshot of a plan**. Anyone can check what you said you would do, and when.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
You need no account today. We are going to *read* OSF the way reviewers do.
:::
::::

::: notes
Before the declaring, the infrastructure. Everything you have touched today – the dataset, my analysis script, the codebook – lives at a permanent public address on the Open Science Framework. OSF does two jobs. It archives materials, which is the only reason you were able to stand in a real analyst's shoes this morning rather than a made-up one. And it registers plans: a registration is a frozen, timestamped snapshot of what you intend to do, filed before you do it, that nobody – including you – can quietly edit afterwards. You do not need an account for any of this today. We are going to read OSF the way a reviewer or a sceptical reader would, starting with this paper's own trail.
:::

## Two templates, one choice

::: {.small}
- Today: the **AsPredicted short form** – eight plain-language questions (on OSF: "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org")
- The fuller tool for our job: the **secondary-data template** (van den Akker et al. 2021, *Meta-Psychology*) – 26 items, built for reanalysing data you already hold
- Both are in your reading; today's block is the short form, adapted for data-in-hand
:::

::: notes
Two templates on the table, and we use one of them. Today it is the AsPredicted short form – eight questions in plain language, the shortest recognised template there is, and completable in the eight minutes we have. But I want you to know its limits. AsPredicted was written for people who have not collected data yet. Its very first question – "have any data been collected?" – has, for us, the awkward answer "it's complicated, I already hold everything". There is a template built precisely for that situation: the secondary-data preregistration template by van den Akker and colleagues, twenty-six items, with a whole section on what you already know about the data. It is in your reading list, and it is the tool a full version of today's exercise would use. Our block borrows its best idea.
:::

## Eight questions, your answers already mapped {.smaller}

| AsPredicted asks | Your block answers |
|---|---|
| Q1 Have data been collected? | "It's complicated – I already hold them" + what I already know |
| Q2 Main question / hypothesis? | the claim, in your one sentence |
| Q3 Dependent variable? | your **outcome** axis |
| Q4 Conditions? | your other five axes, held at baseline |
| Q5 Analyses? | your model + your support/undermine rule |
| Q6 Outliers / exclusions? | your **sample** axis |
| Q7 Sample size? | N = 270 country-years – fixed |
| Q8 Anything else? | your DAG-grounded justification |

::: notes
And here is why the block will take you eight minutes and not forty: you have already done all the thinking. Watch the mapping. The claim sentence you typed in chat before lunch – that is question two. Your outcome axis is the dependent variable, question three. The five axes you are holding at baseline are your conditions. Your sample axis is the exclusion rule. The sample size is fixed by the panel – two hundred and seventy, nobody gets to choose. And the one question AsPredicted fumbles for us, question one, you answer the grown-up way: the data exist, I hold them, and here is what I already know – including that the baseline lands at minus three point eight zero four. The six-axis menu drops straight into the eight boxes. All that is left is to write it down.
:::

## Two sentences worth keeping

::: {.claimcard}
"the common single-path analyses in social and behavioural research should not be simply assumed to be robust to alternative analyses" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]
:::

::: {.claimcard}
A blueprint: precise question → causal reasoning (DAG) → multiverse → sensitivity analysis [@AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial]
:::

::: {.small}
- Same-conclusion robustness and same-*number* robustness are different bars
- Justifiability is the criterion – choose with reasons, show the spread
:::

::: notes
Two sentences to take away. From the Multi100 paper: single-path analyses should not simply be assumed robust. And notice what preregistration did and did not do for you today – it protected your choice from being opportunistic, but it gave your declared dot no special status inside the curve. You lived both halves: the declaration made your one path defensible, and the grid showed it was still just one path among 840. That pairing – declare your path, then show the space it sits in – is the whole method. From Auspurg and Brüderl, the constructive recipe we followed: precise question, explicit assumptions, multiverse, sensitivity. And keep the two robustness standards apart in your own writing: same *conclusion* – seventy-four per cent in Multi100 – and same *number* – thirty-four. When you claim robustness, say which one you mean.
:::
